title: Researchers explore potential of lithium-sulphur batteries - electrive.com
content:
Researchers from Vanderbilt University and the University of Maryland have presented a new cell chemistry that could significantly increase the energy density of lithium-sulphur batteries. By integrating chlorine, the approach enables additional electron transfer at higher voltage.
Grafik: Vanderbilt University
Lithium-sulphur batteries have long been regarded as a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion cells, as sulphur is abundant and can store significantly more charge per unit of weight. However, implementing them in a durable and practical way has proven challenging.
In a study published under
Nature Energy
, a joint team from Vanderbilt University and the University of Maryland describe a new approach in which sulphur participates in an additional energy-storing reaction. The result is a sulphur-based battery that operates at a higher average voltage and stores more charge.
Prototype lithium-sulphur battery stores 1,700 watt-hours of energy
While in conventional systems each sulphur atom exchanges two electrons, the novel system also integrates chlorine to transfer a third electron. In laboratory tests, this increased sulphur’s storage capacity by approximately 58 per cent and raised the average operating voltage from about 2.05 volts to 2.54 volts. By combining enhanced charge storage capacity with higher voltage, one kilogram of sulphur in the experimental test cell was able to store more than 1,700 watt-hours of energy.
To ensure reversibility, the researchers used molecular simulations to design an electrolyte. This keeps the chlorine reactive while simultaneously preventing the resulting sulphur-chlorine product from dissolving and migrating to the lithium-metal anode.
78 per cent capacity retained after 100 charge cycles
Various spectroscopic techniques confirmed that sulphur repeatedly transitions through the new state during charging and discharging. A constructed pouch cell retained 78 per cent of its initial capacity after 100 charge cycles.
However, significant work remains before commercial use, as the prototype uses a lithium-metal anode as well as larger quantities of electrolyte. Taking into account all essential battery components – not just the electrode alone – the scientists estimate that the approach could enable a gravimetric energy density at the cell level of 477 Wh/kg. This would represent a value approximately 37 per cent higher than comparable conventional lithium-sulphur systems.
“The traditional way of thinking about lithium-sulphur batteries leaves some of sulphur’s redox capacity untapped,” said De-en Jiang, Professor of Chemical Engineering and Chemistry at Vanderbilt University and co-corresponding author of the study. “We wanted to see whether we could expand sulphur’s redox capability and use it to store more energy.”

title: Fraunhofer expands South Korean battery research partnership - electrive.com
content:
The Fraunhofer Battery Alliance is expanding its collaboration with partners from South Korea. Two new letters of intent are set to pave the way for joint research projects on battery materials, cell production, and recycling.
Fraunhofer, POSTECH and the city of Pohang reaffirm their collaboration in battery research.
Image: Fraunhofer FFB
During a delegation visit to the Fraunhofer FFB in Münster, two letters of intent were signed with the Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), the city of Pohang, and the Korea Environment Corporation (K-eco).
The focus is on joint research and development activities across the battery value chain. With POSTECH and the city of Pohang, potential topics range from materials for lithium-ion batteries and next-generation battery technologies to cell and production processes, as well as recycling and the circular economy. The city of Pohang is to provide administrative and funding policy support for joint activities with local companies and international research cooperation.
POSTECH already brings expertise in next-generation battery technologies. In early 2026, a research team from the university, together with KAIST and Gyeongsang National University, presented an
anode-free lithium-metal battery
with a volumetric energy density of 1,270 Wh/l. According to the researchers, the cell retained 81.9 per cent of its initial capacity after 100 cycles. The results were also confirmed in larger pouch cells.
Fraunhofer FFB to scale new battery technologies
A central role in the collaboration is played by the Fraunhofer Research Institution for Battery Cell Production (FFB) in Münster. Its concept combines laboratory and production research for cylindrical cells, prismatic cells, and pouch cells. Depending on the project, individual process steps or complete production chains can be examined.
Jens Tübke and Sung Min Kim seal the deal on battery recycling and quality assurance.
For the joint activities, the
FFB PreFab
in Münster-Amelsbüren is available, among other facilities. There, new materials, cell concepts, and manufacturing processes can be tested under near-industrial conditions. The goal is to assess their scalability at an early stage and prepare the transition towards series production or large-scale industrial manufacturing.
“The development of new battery technologies and the establishment of a sustainable battery value chain require close cooperation between research and industry across national borders,” said Jens Tübke, Director of the Fraunhofer FFB and spokesperson for the Fraunhofer Battery Alliance. With the South Korean partners, the aim is to pool scientific expertise and jointly develop solutions for battery cell production and recycling.
The Research Institution for Battery Cell Production is also one of the largest publicly funded battery projects in Germany. The German federal government is providing up to €750 million euros for research facilities and projects at the Fraunhofer FFB, while the state of North Rhine-Westphalia is contributing a further €320 million for land and new buildings. The FFB is embedded in the federal government’s overarching battery research concept.
The second agreement with K-eco places a stronger emphasis on battery recycling, material characterisation, as well as certification and quality assurance procedures for recovered battery materials. In addition, the partners want to explore research approaches that can support compliance with the
EU Battery Regulation
This cooperation addresses an area that, while technically advanced, still faces significant economic challenges. A study within the
EU Safeloop project
recently quantified the current loss in battery recycling at around €1.90 euros per kilogram of battery pack. Key cost drivers include hazardous goods transport, dismantling, and uncertainties in material recovery. Standardised quality and certification procedures could therefore gain importance for establishing viable circular economy models.
No specific joint research projects, timelines, or additional funding volumes were revealed as part of the newly signed agreements.

title: Highlights of the Open Tech Forums at The Battery Show NA
content:
Industry Outlook
Battery News
Explore sessions highlighting advancements in battery technology, energy systems, and sustainable electrification solutions.
October 5, 2026
4 Min Read
Attendees at The Battery Show North America 2025 in Detroit.
Courtesy of The Battery Show.
For attendees of
The Battery Show North America
who may not have time for full-length panel discussions or technical presentations, the
Open Tech Forums
offer a convenient alternative. Sessions are held at Booth 2850 on the exhibition floor; these 25-minute sessions provide concise updates on industry trends and developments. Designed to fit into a busy schedule, the forums are an accessible way to stay informed and gain insights from experts in the battery industry.
Here are some suggested topics and presentations to consider at the Open Tech Forums during the Battery Show North America 2026:
Graphite anode active material: The lesser discussed roadblock to localization of US battery material supply chain
Presented by Prasanna Mantravadi, Manager at
FEV Consulting Inc
., this session explores the critical role of Graphite Anode Active Material (AAM) in the energy transition and the challenges it faces in the
US battery supply chain
. Despite growing domestic cell production, AAM localization faces barriers such as high costs, sustainability concerns, trade tariffs, and project timelines, with China controlling 90% of global production.
Related:
Explore the First 15 Years of The Battery Show
The presentation compares natural and synthetic graphite's performance and costs while exploring strategies to overcome these roadblocks. Attendees will gain insights into fostering domestic AAM production and navigating the complexities of manufacturing and commercialization. Learn more
V4Smart’s ultra-high-power cells: Where precision manufacturing meets extreme performance
Presented by Dr. Verena Drews, Head of R&D at
V4Smart GmbH & Co. KG
, this session explores V4Smart’s advanced cylindrical lithium-ion cell production platform. As one of Europe’s battery manufacturers with an operational mass-production line certified to IATF standards, V4Smart combines automation, precision equipment, and AI-based process optimization to ensure consistent quality and scalability.
presentation
highlights the design and performance of V4Smart’s next-generation cells for applications like electrified mobility and aerospace. Attendees will learn how precision manufacturing turns innovative cell designs into scalable, reliable battery solutions.
Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology allows electric vehicles (EVs) to communicate with the power grid. Courtesy of Toyota Motor North America.
Enabling bidirectional electric vehicles: A global policy and regulatory comparison of V2X adoption
Presented by Olga Bredikhina, Transportation Research Economist and Business Intelligence Manager at
Alabama Mobility and Power Center,
The University of Alabama, this session explores the global landscape of
bidirectional charging
and Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) adoption. It examines regulatory frameworks, technical standards, market structures, and consumer incentives across key markets, including the US, Canada, China, Japan, and Europe.
Related:
Canada Slaps New Tariffs on US Products
presentation
highlights how centralized governance, advanced metering infrastructure, and standardized protocols enable scalable V2X applications, while fragmented regulations and interoperability challenges hinder progress. Attendees will gain insights into integrating EVs as distributed energy resources and accelerating V2X adoption in residential, commercial, and fleet contexts.
Presented by Marcus Peng, Business Development Manager at
Keysight Technologies Inc.
, this session explores the importance of power efficiency in AI data centers and its impact on sustainability and return on investment. The discussion covers modern data center power architectures, including the transition from medium-voltage systems to high-voltage DC approaches like 800 Vdc, which aim to improve efficiency and reduce resource usage.
also addresses safety considerations, component availability, and challenges associated with high-voltage systems. Attendees will learn about measurement methodologies for assessing efficiency under various conditions, providing a comprehensive understanding of next-generation power systems.
Related:
Global EV Sales to Hit 27% of Market in 2026 Despite US Policy Headwinds
As AI data centers grow in size and complexity, their energy demands are skyrocketing. Courtesy of Hugo Kurk, iStock / Getty Images Plus.
Fast-Charging Lithium-Ion Batteries: An Electrode Design Perspective
Presented by Mr. Andre Hugentobler, VP of Technology, Innovation, and New Business Development at
Trinseo Europe GmbH
, this session examines the critical role of electrode architecture in enabling fast-charging lithium-ion batteries. The
discussion
focuses on challenges such as non-uniform lithiation and lithium plating in thicker, high-capacity electrodes, and explores design strategies to address them.
Topics include optimized particle sizes, conductive networks, multilayer coatings, and primer layers to enhance charge uniformity and performance. Attendees will learn how manufacturing processes like drying and calendering affect electrode porosity and ion transport, as well as how binder chemistry (SBR/PAA) influences fast-charge capability.
About the Author
Maria Guerra
Senior Editor-Battery Technology, Informa Markets
Maria L. Guerra is a Senior Editor at
Battery Technology
, blending her engineering background with a passion for technology journalism. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Universidad Metropolitana in Caracas, Venezuela, and a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering.
Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. (KBR) in the UK, conducting power system studies and providing technical support for offshore and onshore projects. During her internship at Pequiven S.A. in Venezuela, she trained neural networks using MATLAB (Kohonen Map) to estimate electrical circuit variables for oil wells (e.g., voltage, current, and power).
In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at
Electronic Design
, covering advancements in the semiconductor market, focusing on power/analog electronics systems.
Battery Technology
, Guerra now delivers in-depth coverage of battery manufacturing, EV advancements, energy storage systems, and the evolving landscape of critical minerals and second-life batteries. She is passionate about uncovering the stories that shape the future of electrification, from cutting-edge battery innovations to policy shifts driving sustainable energy.
Guerra is also a member of
The Battery Show North America Advisory Board
, where she contributes her expertise to advising on industry trends and speaker selection for The Battery Show North America, while helping to shape discussions on battery technology and electrification. She was part of the award-winning Battery Technology team recognized with a
Neal Award for Best Coverage of the 2024 Election
Neal Award for Best Explanatory Content
in 2026 for her coverage of battery breakthroughs.

title: Supply Chain Executive Appointment: Dean Bain Joins Kinaxis
content:
Supply Chain Executive Appointment: Dean Bain Joins Kinaxis
Prioritise Us
on Google
Dean Bain has taken on a new role at Kinaxis
Dean Bain has been appointed Senior Vice President of Sales for North America at Kinaxis, working to make a positive impact in global supply chains
Dean Bain has announced the next step in his career, joining Kinaxis as the Senior Vice President of Sales for North America.
With a vast career in supply chain and sales,
Dean is returning to supply chain planning
, working to help global supply chains.
In a period of ongoing volatility, Dean is eager to use his expertise in order to help leaders unlock their full potential.
Dean's new role at Kinaxis
With a strong career history, having launched his first start-up in 2002 at just 20 years old, Dean has gained significant experience in global supply chain operations. Since then, Dean has worked at various corporations, gaining experience in global teams.
He describes himself as being focused on profitable growth, with exceptional customer service experience and dedication. Throughout his career, he has approached each job with vigour, viewing each opportunity as a personal investment.
As a result, he has undertaken an impressive career route, gaining strong leadership skills and making his way up through the supply chain industry. Within this, he has worked within various industries, learning how each part of the supply chain operates and experiencing them during different periods of volatility.
Now, he has announced a new role at Kinaxis, a global leader in modern supply chain management.
Kinaxis aims to serve supply chains
and those who are making them operate. Its solutions and software help navigate volatility, gain agility and embed AI without using the human touch.
"After an intentional three-month break to focus on family, health and (admittedly) my golf game, I'm pleased to share that today I
officially joined Kinaxis
as SVP Sales, North America," Dean shared to LinkedIn.
"I'm excited to be getting back to my roots in supply chain planning where I've spent most of my career. And after many years working together, it's great to be reunited with Jeff Flammer, Mark Morgan, Razat Gaurav and many others! This team has built some tremendous momentum. I'm grateful for their trust and I can't wait to help increase the octane!
"Looking forward to reconnecting with customers, partners and friends across the industry and continuing to make an impact on Supply Chains across the globe."
Dean has a strong history in supply chain management
Dean's career so far
Dean started his career in 2002, when he founded and led Tool Tech International. He held the role of CEO for almost three years, before joining Tradetec Skyline as Senior Exhibit Sales Representative.
In 2007, he joined DHL as an Account Representative, gaining experience in a globally recognised logistics organisation. Here, he worked with an
expansive team from around the world
, gaining insights into logistics and distribution networks.
Following this, Dean joined UPS, beginning his journey there as Conversion Account Executive. In just over one year, he was promoted to Senior Account Executive, where he lead a team and took on a critical role, bridging the gap between UPS and its clients. In this role, he became even more competent in leadership and strategic planning, working on driving revenue growth and managing complex PR cycles.
In 2012, he began his nine year career at Blue Yonder, where he worked his way up to Vice President, Sales - Discrete Manufacturing. Here, he led commercial strategy and revenue generation for the company, alongside client relationships. As a result, Dean demonstrated his strong capabilities in nurturing relationships and driving growth.
Most recently, Dean worked at Coupa Software, as Senior Vice President Supply Chain. At Coupa, Dean oversaw operations spanning from product strategy to customer support. Having joined in 2023, he has led his team through a
fair amount of disruption
, navigating a volatile landscape with an increasing integration of AI.
Now, Dean will be taking all of his expertise to Kinaxis. Here, he will bring his knowledge of supply chain disruption and digitalisation to the company, working to help clients as they
navigate turbulence
and look towards a more resilient future.
Looking forward to reconnecting with customers, partners and friends across the industry and continuing to make an impact on Supply Chains across the globe.
Dean Bain, SVP Sales, North America at Kinaxis
Key companies
CEO: Razat Gaurav
HQ: Ontario, Canada
Kinaxis is a Canadian supply chain management software company founded in 1984. Its flagship product, RapidResponse, provides cloud-based supply chain planning including demand planning, supply planning, and inventory optimization. The platform enables real-time collaboration and scenario analysis, helping companies respond quickly to supply disruptions. Kinaxis serves industries like automotive, aerospace, high-tech, and life sciences, with clients including major global manufacturers.
CEO: Mile Lipps
HQ: California, US
Coupa Software is a cloud-based business spend management platform founded in 2006. The platform provides procurement, invoicing, expense management, and supply chain solutions. Coupa's unified system helps organizations gain visibility and control over business spending across procurement, suppliers, contracts, and expenses. The company serves enterprises globally, enabling them to optimize spending, improve compliance, and drive substantial savings through digital transformation.
Blue Yonder
CEO: Duncan Angove
HQ: Arizona, US
Blue Yonder, formerly JDA Software, is a supply chain and retail planning solutions provider. Acquired by Panasonic in 2021, it offers AI-driven software for supply chain management, demand forecasting, and warehouse management. The platform leverages machine learning to help businesses optimize operations and improve efficiency. Blue Yonder serves retailers, manufacturers, and logistics providers globally, enabling resilient supply chains through analytics.

title: Microlise: Turning Fleet Data into Supply Chain Performance
content:
Microlise: Turning Fleet Data into Supply Chain Performance
Prioritise Us
on Google
Microlise is driving cost savings and efficiency in global fleets. Credit: Europa Worldwide Group
Microlise is working to navigate supply chain disruption and support its operators as they evolve in a changing world, Microlise CEO Nadeem Raza explains
Around the world, logistics is facing greater challenges than ever before. As organisations come under scrutiny for their sustainability initiatives or their ability to meet customer demand amid volatility, they are turning to new technologies to remain competitive.
Microlise, a technology company specialising in
fleet management solutions
, uses telematics and other critical insights in order to strengthen fleet operations.
With real-time management capabilities, the company helps its clients operate more sustainably, more efficiently and with greater compliance.
Logistics demands
Fleet management is a critical part of modern logistics, no longer just about tracking assets. Now, it includes
driving sustainability initiatives
, cost savings, driver safety and compliance in an increasingly complex environment.
Fleet management data is now a key performance indicator, helping managers optimise performance with real-time data points. It can reduce operating costs by identifying idling and poor driving performance, leading to the reduction of fuel consumption. With an increase in visibility, leaders can now identify problem areas early on and take action.
This also leads to improved driving style across the fleet, meaning incidents are reduced.
Its 2026 Industry Report took insights from transport and logistics professionals about the challenges they are currently facing. Leaders explored how they are investing in technology in order to remain competitive and adapt with accuracy.
“Artificial Intelligence (AI), automation and real-time operational visibility are no longer future concepts,” explains Nadeem Raza, CEO of Microlise.
“They are rapidly becoming embedded within day-to-day fleet management, fundamentally changing how modern fleet businesses operate.
“What we found is a sector becoming more confident, more connected and increasingly driven by data-led decision making. Across the industry, operators are not only embracing tools to improve visibility but are actively seeking ways to simplify complexities and reduce inefficiencies.
“At the same time, the findings also highlight the growing pressure facing businesses still reliant on fragmented systems and manual processes.”
Nadeem Raza, CEO of Microlise
Company statistics
Microlise has more than 42 years of experience
It partners with more than 2,500 customers around the world
Data from customer assets in 195 countries is collected and analysed to offer the best insights
It uses one single and comprehensive system provider
Microlist has more than 933,000 subscriptions
Tesco reached 99% on-time deliveries after implementing Microlise
Cost of fault accident payouts decreased by more than 65% for Europa Worldwide Group after using Microlise
Tesco on-time
As one of the UK’s leading retailers, Tesco operated a significantly complex logistics network, delivering to more than 3,000 stores across the UK. Every day, its Reading distribution centre dispatches up to 500 vehicles.
Due to the high demand and the importance of its deliveries – including its temperature-specific items – it needs to operate in a timely manner with maximised fleet efficiency.
Tesco has more than 2,500 trucks and 4,000 trailers, making it one of the largest LGV fleets in the UK. Managing a network of this scale is a challenge of its own, particularly when it needs to maintain safety standards, temperature regulation, accuracy and timely deliveries.
The retailer integrated Microlise’s advanced technology, making use of a comprehensive suite of software to enhance the management of its fleet. Its key priorities included fleet tracking, to
enhance delivery tracking
, driver performance, to offer real-time feedback on driver safety, and fleet safety management, to monitor fuel usage and lower operational costs.
Since implementation, Tesco has seen significant growth in its delivery performance, reaching 99% on-time deliveries for large stores and 96% for convenience stores. It is also seeing better driving styles and improved safety across its fleet. This has also led to enhanced hazard perception and reduced emissions.
Tesco has a complex supply chain, with products which require temperature control. Credit: Tesco
Increasing safe driving
Europa Worldwide Group has also seen a major transformation within its fleet operations, through using Microlise. The logistics company operates from 26 locations around the world and delivers to 10,000 locations.
It has 30 HGVs and 500 trailers in its network, resulting in up to 2,400 deliveries per day.
The scale and expanse of its fleet, therefore, is an ongoing challenge to manage particularly as global logistics is becoming increasingly complex. Opposing legislation, ongoing trade disputes and geopolitical volatility are all impacting the flow of operations, meaning visibility into the fleet is crucial for
maintaining safety and compliance
Before using Microlise, Europa used a range of tools for in-cab cameras, tachograph downloads, tracking and more. As a result, data was siloed, making it unclear when issues arose or how to cut them off before they got worse.
Worker safety was also a key priority – in 2023, £238,000 (US$315,900) was spent on fault accident pay-outs.
Since adopting Microlise’s range of software – including Journey Management, Multi-camera systems, Co-Pilot, TruFleet and HGV & Trailer Tracking – Europa has much better visibility into its operations. It is now committed to 100% IoD status to all 35 partners by 9am the following day.
Prior to this adoption, approximately 90% of its drivers were in the High or Very High-risk category for driver performance. Now, 99% are in the Very Low or Low risk category, and cost of fault accident payouts has decreased by more than 65%.
Europa Worldwide Group has seen an increase in driver safety since working with Microlise. Credit: Europa Worldwide Group
Across the industry, operators are not only embracing tools to improve visibility but are actively seeking ways to simplify complexities and reduce inefficiencies.
Nadeem Raza, CEO of Microlise
Around the world, companies are seeing significant improvements in their fleet operations, due to greater visibility. Microlise is helping organisations operate safer and more efficiently each day, reducing accidents,
costs and emissions
at once.
Key partners
Microlise
CEO: Nadeem Raza
HQ: Nottingham, UK
Microlise is a UK-based telematics and transport technology company founded in 1982. Specializing in fleet management solutions, the company provides software and hardware for vehicle tracking, route optimization, and driver safety. title: C.H. Robinson and RXO: Transforming Third-Party Logistics

C.H. Robinson and RXO: Transforming Third-Party Logistics
Prioritise Us
on Google
C.H. Robinson is hoping to acquire RXO. Credit: C.H. Robinson
In an ongoing effort to transform its North American third-party logistics capabilities, C.H. Robinson will acquire RXO, CEO Dave Bozeman explains
C.H. Robinson has announced it is acquiring RXO in a stock-and-cash transaction for an implied value of US$5.8bn.
acquisition will strengthen
C.H. Robinson’s multimodal capabilities, particularly within North America.
The acquisition means the company will be able to reach a larger customer base with greater efficiency and long-term resilience.
Joining logistics offerings
Logistics is becoming increasingly complex and global. Ensuring a reliable footprint in each region is critical when developing a resilient logistics strategy. Organisations like C.H. Robinson need to have strong offerings, demonstrating themselves as having a wide network for its customer base.
C.H. Robinson is an American transportation company
which has a selection of third-party logistics offerings. It offers freight transportation, warehousing, intermodal and less than truckload capabilities.
RXO is an asset-light transportation provider that uses third-party capacity, scale and technology to move freight for its customer base. C.H. Robinson has announced it is entering a definitive agreement with RXO, of which Robinson will acquire RXO. The proposed acquisition, in a transaction with an implied value of US$5.8bn, will result in a combined company with an enterprise value of more than US$25bn.
Through acquiring RXO, C.H. Robinson will be undertaking a stronger and more diverse network, with a multi-modal platform and an accelerated growth strategy. With the capabilities of RXO being absorbed into C.H. Robinson’s network, it now has more modes and segments within the industry.
“This transaction is a natural
next step in our transformation
, allowing us to create a more scaled, resilient North American third-party logistics provider positioned to offer exceptional customer service and redefine the future of our industry,” says Dave Bozeman, C.H. Robinson President and Chief Executive Officer.
Dave Bozeman, CEO of C.H. Robinson
Key numbers
The acquisition has an implied value of US$5.8bn
Combined, C.H. Robinson and RXO will have an enterprise value of more than US$25bn
57% of the merger consideration is paid in cash
RXO stockholders are expected to own 11% of the combined company at the end of the transaction
Gaining new capabilities
C.H. Robinson will be in ownership of both companies’ trucking brokerage and transportation businesses. It will be making use of its own global forwarding expertise, alongside RXO’s strong capabilities in expedited and last mile operations.
This combined network and reach will result in a larger and more comprehensive offering for customers across a larger and denser network.
C.H. Robinson’s Lean AI operating model
, which has proven to be successfully implemented across RXO operations, will unlock new potential within the company.
The company expects to see approximately US$300m of net run-rate cost synergies within two years post-close. This boost in productivity will lead to greater resilience and improved margins. C.H. Robinson is expected to undergo a period of profitable growth, due to these new capabilities.
“Like Robinson, RXO is a customer-focused company with expertise and talent that will allow us to expand our capabilities to better support customers of all sizes on their most complex challenges. By applying our proven Lean AI model to RXO’s business, we expect to significantly enhance productivity to unlock compelling cost synergies,” explains Dave.
“We are confident our experienced team and disciplined execution plan will allow us to seamlessly integrate our organisations and position the combined company to capture the expected synergies, drive innovation and deepen customer relationships to enhance profitable
growth and shareholder value
The Lean AI model is expected to reveal cost-to-serve opportunities, operating efficiencies, shared-service savings and spend optimisation across third-party operations. Through this, the company aims to gain more shareholder value creation and an increased operating leverage.
C.H. Robinson also expects to see faster and more precise AI-driven sales, alongside improved procurement capabilities.
C.H. Robinson will gain new capabilities and an expanded network. Credit: Getty Images
Supply chain diversification
C.H. Robinson is expecting to see an improvement to its network density and capabilities, due to the additional staff and resources from the acquisition. Through this, there will be an increase in verticals and volumes that can be delivered.
With an increase in diversity of customers, there will be increased market visibility across the brand.
“Joining C.H. Robinson represents an exciting next chapter for our company, our employees and our customers. We have built a strong business by staying relentlessly focused on our customers, operating with agility and delivering solutions that help them navigate an
increasingly complex supply chain
,” explains Drew Wilkerson, RXO Chairman and Chief Executive Officer.
“By bringing together our complementary capabilities, talented teams and shared commitment to service, we will be able to offer customers greater scale, broader capabilities and even more value. I’m incredibly proud of what our team has built and excited about the opportunities ahead as part of C.H. Robinson.”
The expanded capabilities will result in better, more tailored multi-modal solutions. Due to those new capabilities, customer and stakeholder relationships will improve, as C.H. Robinson will be able to offer more solutions that are personalised to the customer.
The merger is anticipated to close in the first half of 2027.
Drew Wilkerson, RXO Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
This transaction is a natural next step in our transformation, allowing us to create a more scaled, resilient North American third-party logistics provider positioned to offer exceptional customer service and redefine the future of our industry.

content:

is expected to reveal the new iX4 this week. Ahead of its debut, images of the new iX4 leaked online, offering an early look.
Leaked images reveal the new BMW iX4
The all-new iX4 is almost here. BMW said the new electric coupe-SUV will go on sale by the end of 2026.
Following the iX3 and i3, the iX4 will replace the current X4 with BMW’s updated Neue Klasse design and technology.
The 2027 BMW iX4 will be available in two versions: the 40 xDrive and 50 xDrive. Both are all-wheel drive (AWD), but will offer different performance and range options.
It will essentially be a sportier, more crossover-like sibling to the new iX3 SUV. Like the iX3 and i3, the iX4 will use BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive and a 108.7 kWh battery.
The 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive offers a WLTP range of up to 500 miles (805 km). In the US, it uses a 112.2-kWh battery, providing an EPA-estimated range of up to 434 miles.

A post shared by CocheSpias (@cochespias1)
While BMW has yet to confirm a specific debut date, we know the iX4 will make its first appearance this fall. With its debut just around the corner, leaked images of the new iX4 by
@Kero_Wolf
apparently reveal the interior and exterior.
The images show a design similar to the
disguised prototypes
spotted testing over the past several months.
BMW iX3 50 xDrive (Source: BMW)
With a rakish roofline, BMW’s new iX4 looks more like a grand tourer than a traditional SUV like the iX3. It trades the boxy SUV look for a sporty, fastback-like silhouette.
Inside, the new iX4 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup includes a 17.9″ central touchscreen, a newly designed steering wheel, and the BMW Panoramic Vision 3D Head-Up Display that stretches across the dashboard.

title: Tesla sold under 1,000 cars in its first year in India, but it's ramping
content:
Tesla Model Y
Tesla Model YL
Fred Lambert
| Oct 6 2026 - 6:58 am PT
Tesla has registered just 993 vehicles in India since it started deliveries there in September 2025, according to registration data compiled by Indian EV publication
ElecTree
But 294 of those came in September 2026 alone. That’s a record month for Tesla in India, and it comes right after the automaker cut prices and launched the six-seat Model Y L.
Tesla needed nine months to sell 428 cars
launched in India in July 2025
with a Model Y priced at roughly $70,000, almost twice what it cost in the US at the time. We said the price didn’t make sense.
The numbers agreed. Tesla registered 69 cars in September 2025, its first month of deliveries, and it didn’t beat that figure for the next eight months. It finished 2025 with 226 registrations and added only 202 more between January and May 2026, per ElecTree’s count. February was the low point at 29 cars.
A note on the “first year” math. The data covers 13 calendar months, September 2025 through September 2026. Count only the first 12 and Tesla is at 699 cars.
These are also registrations, not deliveries. Tesla doesn’t report sales by country, so registrations are the closest thing we get.
A price cut and the Model Y L changed the trend
Tesla made two moves this spring.
On April 22, it launched the Model Y L in India at ₹61.99 lakh (about $65,000), with deliveries starting in June. The longer six-seater came in cheaper than the five-seat Model Y Long Range, which was listed at ₹67.89 lakh (about $71,000) and has since been dropped from the lineup.
Then in late May, Tesla cut the entry-level Model Y by ₹9 lakh, from ₹59.89 lakh to ₹50.89 lakh. That’s a 15% cut, and it brings the starting price to about $53,000.
Registrations took off from there:
Month (2026)
Model Y L
Entry Model Y
Tesla total
September
That’s 565 registrations in four months, more than the 428 Tesla managed in its first nine.
The Model Y L is doing most of the work. It has 425 registrations in four months, which is exactly what the entry-level Model Y has put up in 13. In September, the six-seater accounted for 81% of Tesla’s registrations in India.
Model Y L launched in the US in July at $61,990
. So before taxes and fees, Indian buyers are paying within about $3,000 of the US price for an imported car, in a country with import duties of up to 110%. A year ago, Tesla was asking them to pay almost double.
It’s still a lot more than the roughly $47,000 the Model Y L launched at in China, where Tesla builds it.
Tesla has also added locations. It started with showrooms in Mumbai, Delhi, and Gurugram, and ElecTree reports that it has since opened in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, and Noida.
Tesla is still a rounding error in India
India registered 35,995 electric cars in September, up 98% from a year ago, according to
Vahan registration data reported by Autocar Professional
. Tata alone did 14,769. Tesla’s record month works out to 0.8% of India’s EV market.
Tesla looks better in the luxury segment. The same data has BMW at 502 electric cars in September, Tesla at 291, and Mercedes-Benz at 125.
So Tesla is now the second-biggest luxury EV brand in India with about 30% of the segment, up from 69 cars in the same month last year.
The comparison that stings is VinFast. The Vietnamese automaker registered its first cars in India the same month Tesla did. But it assembles them at a plant in Tamil Nadu, and it prices its SUVs between ₹18 lakh and ₹23 lakh (about $19,000 to $24,000).
VinFast registered 2,963 cars in India in September. That’s three times what Tesla has done in 13 months, in a single month.
Different price class, obviously. But it shows what building locally gets you in India.
Electrek’s Take
In January, we wrote that you can’t sell a $40,000 car for $70,000 and expect volume. Tesla tried it anyway and got 40 to 60 cars a month.
Then it cut the entry price by 15%, brought in a bigger car for less than the old top trim, and now it’s at almost 300 a month.
It must be a bit confusing for the Indian consumer.
It’s also hard to tell how much price changes affect volume compared to expansions in other cities.
Either way, for now, it looks like Tesla is not giving up on the Indian market despite the lackluster performance.

title: Kia EV3 first drive: the affordable EV we have been waiting for
content:
The Kia EV3 starts at $29,890 in the US, and after a day of driving it around Vancouver Island, I think it’s the best-packaged affordable EV you can buy right now.
It comes with up to 321 miles of range, two battery sizes, and available all-wheel drive, which is more choice than anything else at this price. But there’s a catch: that $30,000 price tag climbs fast.
Kia brought me to Vancouver Island last week to test the EV3 as it launches in North America.
The Korean automaker took its time. The EV3 has been on sale overseas since 2024, and it quickly became one of the most popular EVs in Europe and won the 2025 World Car of the Year award before Kia finally decided to bring it here.
Now it’s here. US sales started in mid-August, and Kia told us it has about 1,300 units in dealer stock. According to the company, dealers love it because it’s bringing more shoppers into showrooms.
A Bolt EV with more options
Kia sees the EV3 as a competitor to the Chevy Bolt and the Nissan Leaf. Those are pretty much your only other choices if you want a new EV around $30,000 in the US.
The 2027 Bolt starts at $28,995 with 262 miles of range, and the 2026 Leaf starts at $29,990 with up to 303 miles. The EV3 lands right between them at $29,890 before a $1,495 destination fee.
The way I see it, the EV3 is really a Bolt EV that’s better packaged and comes with more options. You get to pick between two battery packs, front-wheel or all-wheel drive, and five trims, so you can end up with something closer to what you really want. Neither the Bolt nor the Leaf offers AWD.
The base Light FWD comes with a 58.3 kWh pack that’s good for 221 miles. For $34,990, the Wind FWD gets the 81.4 kWh pack and the full 321 miles. All-wheel drive adds a second motor for 261 hp and brings range down to 280 miles. At the top, the $45,890 GT makes 288 hp and gets to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds.
The EV3 also takes over from the Niro EV, which started at $39,700 with 253 miles of range. So Kia’s entry-level EV just got about $10,000 cheaper.
Small footprint, big battery
The EV3 is a boxy-looking compact SUV with Kia’s “tiger face” front end and the same design language as the EV6 and EV9.
Boxy usually means bad aero. But Kia focused on aero optimization and got the drag coefficient down to 0.275.
That’s a big reason why the base version gets impressive range out of a relatively small pack. And Kia still managed to fit a big 81.4 kWh pack into a vehicle that’s just 169.3 inches long. According to Kia, the new pack has 22% higher energy density than the one in the Niro EV.
The EV3 rides on a 400-volt version of the E-GMP platform, so don’t expect EV6 charging speeds. Peak rates are about 100 kW and 127 kW depending on the pack, but peak charge rates aren’t the whole story. At virtually any DC fast-charging station, you’ll be able to charge to 80% in roughly 30 minutes. Kia says that’s about 30% faster than the Niro EV.
It comes with a NACS port and Plug & Charge, which Kia says gives you access to more than 40,000 DC fast chargers.
Inside, you get 26 cubic feet of cargo space behind the rear seats and about 56 cubic feet with them folded.
There’s also a 0.9 cubic-foot frunk. It’s small, but we often don’t see any frunk on a vehicle of this form factor, and Kia says it’s the only one in this segment. We appreciate Kia making the effort.
Kia says the EV3 has 99.7 cubic feet of passenger volume, which it claims is more than any of its direct competitors.
When I sat in the back seat, I felt I had plenty of legroom with the front seat at a normal position, but when sitting straight, my head was within 3 inches of the ceiling (I’m 6ft tall).
The tech is what you’d expect from a more expensive EV: over-the-air updates, Apple CarPlay, and apps like YouTube and Netflix. Highway Driving Assist is standard on every trim, and a head-up display is available on the GT.
One thing to watch: vehicle-to-load (V2L) isn’t available below the GT-Line. On the trims that have it, Kia includes the external adapter.
Driving the EV3
Kia sent us on a loop out of Victoria: north over the Malahat, west to Port Renfrew, and back along the coast. I drove the Wind FWD and the GT-Line AWD.
The driving experience is impressive for an entry-level EV. The FWD version makes 201 hp and the AWD makes 261 hp. I never felt like I didn’t have enough power in either of them.
The EV3 also felt planted on the road, even on the tough logging roads around Vancouver Island. For a vehicle in that segment, I was pleasantly surprised by the driving experience.
Every EV3 gets four-wheel independent suspension, and Kia adds acoustic laminated glass on the windshield and front windows from the Wind trim up.
Then there’s one-pedal driving, and it feels great. Kia’s new i-Pedal 3.0 gives you three regen levels, and you turn it on by pulling and holding the left paddle.
And Kia finally remembers your preferred setting between drives. If you’ve owned a Kia or Hyundai EV, you know how annoying it was to turn i-Pedal back on every time you got in the car.
The price goes up fast
My main concern is the “affordable” part.
It’s true that you can get an EV3 for $30,000. But the cheapest version I tested was still $41,000, and the GT-Line AWD starts at $43,490. The price goes up fast depending on the options, so be on the lookout for that.
The good news is that you don’t have to go that high. You can get the base version for $29,890, or the max range in a well-equipped Wind FWD for $34,990. That one looks like the sweet spot of the lineup.
Electrek’s Take
This is the affordable EV we have been waiting for.
To be fair, the bar isn’t high. The other choices around $30,000 are very limited, with just the Bolt EV and the Leaf. But the EV3 gives you more than either of them: two battery sizes, up to 321 miles of range, and AWD if you need it.
It’s a Bolt EV that’s better packaged, with enough optionality to get you closer to the vehicle you really want. And that’s from someone who likes the Bolt EV.
Top comment by OliveFries
We really wanted a Kia EV3 to replace our second car but after our first Kia EV9 ownership experience we're looking at different options. Our Kia dealership and more importantly Kia America experiences have completely turned us away from wanting to own another one. Our EV9 was down for 2 months after the rear motor failed with only a few thousand miles and somehow it wasn't available. After some time sitting at the shop I opened a case with Kia America to assist. They had a single phone call with me and one with the dealership then did absolutely nothing. Nobody could get ahold of the case manager until after I already had the car back (over a month).
They then told me they'd take care of the car payments as a "goodwill" gesture for the down time only to find out I had to completely waive my lemon law rights for this and any future repairs on the vehicle. This supposedly also includes a non-disparagement agreement. Nothing about it was "goodwill", it was purely to keep me silent about my experience.
Absolutely disgusting behavior.
My worry is the pricing. If most of the EV3s on dealer lots look like the $41,000 one I drove, a lot of buyers will never see the “affordable EV” Kia is advertising. The $30,000 and $35,000 versions are the ones that matter.
But I think this can be a popular vehicle in North America like it already is in Europe. Kia sold 514 of them in the first full month, and I expect that number to go up from here as long as the Korean brand is making them available.
What do you think? Would you take the EV3 over the Bolt or the Leaf? Let us know in the comment section below.

title: This funky solar electric scooter could handle your commute without ever plugging in
content:
Electric Motorcycles
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Oct 6 2026 - 6:11 am PT
There are plenty of ways to build a small electric vehicle. These days, the prevailing options have been to make it faster, give it more power, slap on bigger tires, or keep adding features until your humble little scooter has somehow turned into a 150-pound electric motorcycle.
Or you can be brave and go in the other direction to ask a simpler question: How much vehicle do people actually need for all those short trips around town?
That’s essentially the idea behind the Lightfoot, a wonderfully weird new solar-powered electric scooter from San Francisco R&D company Otherlab. The two-seat electric scooter tops out at just under 20 mph (32 km/h), carries a surprisingly large amount of cargo, and covers both sides of its body in solar panels capable of adding up to 18 miles (29 km) of range per day.
And as someone who has long argued that
we need more small electric vehicles
– not simply faster and heavier e-bikes and e-mopeds – I’m pretty intrigued.
The Lightfoot has actually been kicking around for a while, and I covered
the prototype’s unveiling
nearly two years ago. But now it’s finally available for sale and delivery. The first 100 Launch Edition scooters
are priced at $4,495 including delivery
, with a refundable $100 reservation required to get in line. Those initial scooters will be available in sky blue and solar orange. A bit on the nose, but I like it.
Sure, $4.5k certainly isn’t cheap for a 20 mph electric scooter.
But then again, there aren’t many other electric scooters that can recharge themselves while you’re buying groceries, or fit 45 liters (1.6 cubic feet) of those groceries inside their body panels on the ride home instead of wearing a hiking backpack full of grains and veggies.
Yes, those solar panels actually do something
The most visually obvious feature of the Lightfoot is the pair of 120W solar panels built directly into the sides of the scooter.
Together, the 240W system can add a claimed 3-4 miles (5-6 km) of range per hour in good sunlight, or as much as 18 miles (29 km) over the course of a day.
That’s actually a meaningful amount of solar charging for this type of vehicle.
The trick is that Lightfoot doesn’t require much energy in the first place. Its 52V and 1,560Wh battery is rated for up to 37 miles (60 km) of range. That means someone commuting 5 miles (8 km) each way and leaving the scooter parked outside all day could theoretically replenish most or even all of their daily energy from sunlight under favorable conditions.
Of course, let’s keep the solar thing in perspective. A 1.5 kWh battery isn’t exactly an electric Hummer battery pack. Lightfoot includes a 230W onboard charger and can be plugged into a normal wall outlet, with a full charge taking around four hours. So that means sunshine isn’t necessary to make the scooter practical; it simply gives owners another option.
But there’s something undeniably cool about owning a vehicle that you might rarely need to plug in if your daily trips are short enough.
Sure, there may be downsides. It looks like a strong crosswind could have you tacking back and forth across the lane like a sailboat, and I’m sure they’ve got a solution for locking up – but I can’t quite imagine what it would be with no exposed frame members. But hey, it looks like an engineer’s dream – and I’m an engineer.
More than just a solar science experiment
Fortunately, Lightfoot seems to have put some thought into the rest of the scooter, too.
Power comes from a pair of 750W nominal geared hub motors – one in each wheel – rated at 1,000W peak each. Lightfoot claims a whopping 160 Nm of combined torque, meaning most hills shouldn’t be a problem.
The important takeaway though is that this isn’t supposed to be a high-speed machine. All that motor is there to haul people and cargo up those hills while keeping the speed below 20 mph (32 km/h). Again, they’re pitching this as a bike lane solution, not an electric motorcycle.
There’s also full suspension, with a 70mm-travel inverted front fork and a 45mm-travel rear coil-over shock. Tektro hydraulic disc brakes with 160mm rotors provide stopping power, while chunky 14 x 3.2-inch tires should help soak up rough pavement.
And despite its scooter-sized footprint, this isn’t exactly a featherweight. The lightfoot weighs 141 lb (64 kg) and has a 48-inch wheelbase.
Some of that heft buys you a feature I really like, such as that 45 liter (1.5 cubic foot) lockable, weatherproof cargo compartment inside the body. Lightfoot says that’s enough for three grocery bags.
Even better, there’s room for a passenger. The long bench seat is designed for two riders, meaning this isn’t merely a funky commuter. It can handle a grocery run and then pick someone up on the way home without forcing you to choose between your passenger and your pasta.
Though I will say that the thin PU seat cushion looks roughly as plush as an extra-absorbent maxi pad. Perhaps it’s more comfortable than it looks. I’d certainly be fascinated to find out.
Lighting includes a 2,000-lumen headlight, accelerometer-activated taillight, and a rather serious 120 dB horn. There’s also a lockable center stand, Bluetooth-enabled display, and regenerative braking.
What about those bike lanes?
This is where things become slightly more complicated.
Otherlab pitches Lightfoot as a vehicle for both city streets and bike lanes and says it doesn’t require a license or registration.
But micromobility regulations vary significantly by state and municipality, so riders should check their local laws rather than assuming a sub-20 mph (32 km/h) top speed automatically makes Lightfoot legal everywhere a bicycle can go.
Conceptually, though, that’s clearly the territory Lightfoot is aiming for. This isn’t a 50 mph (80 km/h) Sur-Ron competitor masquerading as an e-bike. It’s a sub-20 mph seated scooter intended for the same sort of short urban trips already being made on electric kick scooters and other low-speed micromobility vehicles.
So as long as there aren’t some disqualifiers like the lack of pedals, it should be fairly easy to fit into the expanding definitions of micromobility vehicles in most places.
Electrek’s Take
I love this idea.
Not necessarily because I think everyone needs solar panels hanging off the sides of their scooter, but because I think we desperately need more experimentation in the space between an e-bike and a car.
There are millions of trips where a 4,500 lb (2,000 kg) automobile is ridiculous overkill, yet people still want weather-protected storage, the ability to carry a passenger, enough torque for hills, and something they can simply hop on and ride.
Lightfoot checks a surprising number of those boxes.
It’s admittedly expensive.
At $4,495
, you’re paying significantly more than many 20 mph (32 km/h) seated electric scooters, including machines like the Infinite Machine Olto. And unlike the Olto, which
can be unlocked
to around 36 mph (55 km/h), Lightfoot isn’t secretly offering you a faster vehicle underneath its low-speed settings. At least, not that I know of.
But speed isn’t really the point here.
You’re paying for the unusual design, the big enclosed cargo compartment, two-person capability, full suspension, dual motors, and – obviously – those giant solar panels.
If all you need is something with two wheels that travels 20 mph, I don’t think Lightfoot makes much financial sense. There are much cheaper ways to accomplish that.
But if your daily mileage is low enough that you could genuinely run largely on sunshine, you’ve got somewhere outdoors to park it, and you want a highly practical little vehicle that looks like absolutely nothing else on the road, then I can see the appeal.
The bigger question is whether enough people are willing to pay a premium for that appeal. Otherlab has built an interesting answer to the question of what a short-trip, self-sustaining vehicle could look like. Now we’ll get to find out whether there are enough buyers asking the same question.

title: Wireless bipolar electrodes raise zinc-air battery power by 80% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Spain and Argentina have developed a zinc-air battery architecture that increases power output by up to 80% by reducing internal resistance without changing the device’s core chemistry.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Researchers at the Institute of Materials Science of Barcelona (ICMAB-CSIC), working with the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) and the National University of La Plata in Argentina, have developed a zinc-air battery architecture that increases power output by up to 80% without changing its core chemistry.
The work, “
Unlocking high power in membraneless Zn-air batteries: A paradigm shift via wireless bipolar electrochemistry
,” was published in August in
Energy Storage Materials
. It challenges the conventional approach of avoiding conductive materials in the electrolyte to prevent short circuits. In the new architecture, conductive elements remain disconnected from the external circuit, while their polarization under an electric field reduces internal resistance rather than causing a short circuit.
The architecture introduces small conductive elements inside the battery that are not connected by wires to either the main electrodes or the external circuit. These elements act as wireless bipolar electrodes and modify the distribution of charge within the device.
The principle relies on the electric field that develops between the two electrodes while the battery is operating. When an electrically isolated conductive element is introduced into the electrolyte, the field polarizes it, causing one end to become positively charged and the other negatively charged. The element thereby creates additional pathways for charge transport without establishing a direct electrical connection between the electrodes.
The effect is particularly relevant to zinc-air batteries, in which the electrochemical reaction involving oxygen limits the rate of operation. Zinc has a favorable oxidation reaction and the system uses aqueous chemistry, while the oxygen reaction is slower and can limit the power the device can deliver.
The wireless bipolar electrodes facilitate charge transport through the electrolyte and reduce losses associated with internal resistance. According to the study, the modification can increase power output by up to 80%.
The system does not require changes to the battery’s main electrochemical materials, instead modifying its internal architecture. This could address a key limitation of zinc-air batteries through an additional physical mechanism alongside the active chemistry.
The authors suggest that the concept could be extended to other energy storage technologies.

title: Japan proposes four categories for priority commercial solar support - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Japan wants to prioritize future subsidies for new commercial solar projects it considers compatible with local communities, as ground-mounted plants lose feed-in tariff (FIT) and feed-in premium (FIP) support from April 2027.
Brian Publicover
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Japan’s Agency for Natural Resources and Energy (ANRE) has proposed keeping feed-in support for commercial solar on land owned by national or local governments, in projects approved under municipal decarbonization plans, on solar carports, and in infrastructure such as airports, roads, railways, and ports.
ANRE presented the proposal in late September to a government renewable energy panel that reports to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI).
New ground-mounted commercial solar will
lose FIT and FIP support from April 1, 2027
, under rules Japan promulgated at the end of the 2025 fiscal year. The cut follows a
package of measures on large-scale solar plants
approved by Cabinet ministers in December 2025 and recommendations from the Procurement Price Calculation Committee in February. Rooftop solar already receives preferential treatment, and the agency is now selecting which other commercial categories should keep support.
The agency assessed 10 candidate categories put forward by ministries, local governments, and industry groups including the Japan Photovoltaic Energy Association (JPEA). It applied three tests covering importance for future deployment, compatibility with local communities, and suitability for the FIT and FIP schemes. The deployment test draws on potential estimates and Japan’s Seventh Strategic Energy Plan, while the scheme test requires a category that can be defined objectively through documents and is expected to export power to the grid.
To pass the community test, a project must either involve no new land development or major change in land use, or be overseen by national or local government for its full operating life, with the power to correct problems.
Conditions attached
Public land qualifies only when the government leases it out or runs the project itself. Land sold to developers would not qualify, because oversight could lapse. Ponds owned by neighborhood associations are excluded, as they do not pass through approval by a mayor or local assembly.
Projects inside municipal renewable promotion zones qualify only if they hold an approved regional decarbonization promotion project plan under the Act on Promotion of Global Warming Countermeasures. Location in a zone alone is not enough. Projects with approved facility plans under Japan’s law on renewable energy in agricultural, forestry, and fishing areas would be treated the same way.
For solar carports, the agency asked the subcommittee whether support could encourage construction of new standalone parking lots, such as monthly or coin-operated lots. Infrastructure covers airports, roads, railways, and ports. Urban parks are excluded because ground-mounted panels are not expected there.
Excluded categories
The agency proposed no priority support for industrial parks and commercial sites, saying the categories lack a uniform definition and offer no guarantee that existing land use would continue. It also excluded former golf courses, former ski resorts, and abandoned farmland, citing the tree felling, topsoil removal, and grading that projects on such land can involve. Projects defined by supplying local utilities, municipalities, or emergency power during disasters were also excluded, because those benefits cannot be verified objectively and do not by themselves prevent safety, landscape, or environmental problems.
The agency deferred a decision on agrivoltaics. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries is preparing
rules defining “desirable” agrivoltaic projects
, including shading below 30%, ground clearance of at least 3 meters, and support spacing of at least 4 meters. The agency proposed giving priority to implementing those rules and continuing to consider agrivoltaics in the next fiscal year.
The 30% shading cap has drawn criticism. In August, the Japan Renewable Energy Foundation (JREF)
called on the agriculture ministry to review the threshold
, citing farms that kept more than 80% of their yields at shading rates above 30%. Japan had approved 6,137 agrivoltaic sites covering 1,361.6 hectares of farmland by the end of fiscal 2023, according to the ministry.
The proposals still require detailed design. Certification criteria, the split between FIT and FIP, auction rules, and support prices and periods will go to the subcommittee and the Procurement Price Calculation Committee between October and January, according to a schedule the agency set out in June. Public comment on the revised ordinances is planned for February and March 2027, with the changes taking effect on April 1, 2027.
Agency estimates put FIT- and FIP-supported capacity at 54.6 GW for ground-mounted commercial solar and 6.1 GW for commercial rooftop, derived by applying the ground-mounted and rooftop split for projects certified since 2017 to total commercial capacity, alongside 17.3 GW for residential systems. A study cited by the agency, led by the Institute of Energy Economics, Japan, puts remaining potential at 137.2 GW for commercial rooftops and 20 GW to 107 GW for ground-mounted sites.

title: German startup offers AI platform to accelerate battery storage engineering - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
German startup Morreon has developed an AI-based platform to streamline engineering, design optimization, tendering, and project scheduling for battery storage and other energy infrastructure projects. The system automates data processing and layout planning while maintaining human oversight, with further integration of cost calculations and construction management planned.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
German engineering startup Morreon GmbH is developing an AI-based operating system designed to accelerate the planning and execution of complex energy infrastructure projects. The platform, called Anchor, combines document processing, engineering design, cost management, tendering, and project scheduling in a single environment.
The company targets battery energy storage systems (BESS), substations, electric truck charging infrastructure, and data centers, where fragmented documentation, repeated design changes, and coordination between engineering disciplines can significantly extend development timelines.
The first stage of the platform focuses on converting unstructured project information into a standardized engineering brief. Anchor processes inputs including PDFs, CAD files, spreadsheets, emails, site documentation, and meeting transcripts. The system classifies information according to its reliability and scope before organizing it within a version-controlled data structure tailored to the relevant infrastructure asset.
“Every extracted value carries full traceability, complete with a confidence level and a direct citation back to the source passage,” said Morreon CEO and founder Alex Zwilling told
pv magazine
, noting that, rather than automatically resolving conflicting inputs, the system flags contradictions for human review. Missing information is converted into prioritized questions assigned to the relevant engineering disciplines.
“To ensure absolute engineering integrity, the system never silently overwrites data; instead, contradictions trigger intelligent proposals for human review, and knowledge gaps transform into prioritized, discipline-tagged questions,” Zwilling explained, adding that engineers must explicitly approve assumptions before they become part of the verified project dataset. According to the company, this creates a consistent information base that can be reused throughout subsequent planning stages.
Automated layouts and design alternatives
Once the engineering brief has been established, Anchor supports the development and comparison of alternative infrastructure layouts. The software maps project information onto dimensionally accurate site plans, allowing engineers to position equipment such as battery containers, transformers, and power conversion systems according to their actual physical dimensions.
“Instead of managing static, disconnected blueprints, architects and engineers can dynamically reposition equipment on the plan, watching power pathways automatically re-route in real time from the grid connection through transformers and power conversion units,” Zwilling said.
Cable lengths and equipment positions are tracked as numerical quantities rather than merely represented as drawing elements. The platform can also generate initial layout arrangements, giving engineers a starting point for evaluating equipment placement and spatial constraints. “This allows teams to compare multiple configurations within seconds, permanently anchoring positions in metric data as baseline documents evolve,” Zwilling added.
Linking design decisions to project costs
Morreon is also working to establish a closer connection between engineering layouts and project budgets. Instead of treating infrastructure components as static elements in drawings, Anchor represents battery blocks, transformers, and cable runs as structured quantities. Changes to a layout therefore update measurable parameters, including cable lengths, equipment requirements, and spatial footprints.
For cost calculations, Morreon uses pricing information from actual supplier quotations and itemized tenders rather than generic benchmark databases. Currently, engineers can assess design modifications against supplier bids, supported by an impact-mapping function that identifies which documents and cost items require updating. A fully automated link between design quantities and tender prices remains under development.
“Morreon’s roadmap directly links those granular tender prices to the design dataset’s quantities,” said Zwilling, highlighting that the planned functionality would allow developers to assess the financial implications of adding equipment or modifying infrastructure layouts during early-stage planning.
The platform also integrates tender preparation, bid evaluation, and project scheduling. Using the verified engineering dataset, Anchor can assemble requests for quotations (RFQs), including technical specifications, procurement scopes, and supplier information. Supplier quotations submitted as PDFs are extracted and organized into structured comparison tables, allowing project teams to evaluate competing bids without manually transferring individual line items into spreadsheets.
“From this single source of truth, the system assembles formal RFQs, incorporating technical specs, scopes, and target suppliers, while automatically ingesting supplier offer PDFs directly into a structured bid comparison matrix,” Zwilling explained.
The same project data supports scheduling and can be exported to tools such as Microsoft Excel and MS Project. Confidentiality controls are designed to prevent commercially sensitive supplier information from crossing unauthorized boundaries. The integrated workflow currently covers the pre-construction process, from initial project intake and engineering through tendering, contract award, and scheduling.
Morreon plans to extend the data flow into purchase orders, delivery tracking, construction supervision, and commissioning. “The ultimate goal is a continuous, error-free thread from initial design through commissioning, ensuring what is planned, ordered, and built always align seamlessly without a single re-typed spreadsheet,” Zwilling said.
Engineers retain final responsibility
Despite the increased level of automation, Morreon emphasizes that professional engineers remain responsible for critical technical and regulatory decisions. Extracted engineering values must be reviewed, assumptions require explicit approval, and unresolved questions cannot be automatically filled with generated information. Tender actions and final project deliverables are also subject to human authorization.
“At Morreon, artificial intelligence acts as a powerful catalyst and draft generator, but the final professional authority and accountability remain strictly in human hands,” Zwilling said.
The company distinguishes between tasks according to the potential consequences of errors. Lower-risk administrative processes can be automated more extensively, while structural design, architectural layouts, and other safety-critical decisions remain subject to stricter human supervision.
Morreon is also building a knowledge base from historical project decisions, enabling the platform to identify recurring configurations and highlight situations requiring additional engineering attention. Source-level traceability, version control, and data storage within EU jurisdictions form part of its approach to compliance. The company is also
bauvorlageberechtigt
in Germany, meaning it is authorized to submit building permit applications directly.

title: Poland unveils new home storage subsidy  - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Poland’s latest subsidy scheme will offer existing prosumers support to purchase and install home storage units. The PLN 1 billion ($258 million) funding call opens for applications on October 20.
Patrick Jowett
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Poland’s Minister of Climate and Environment Paulina Hennig-Kloska
Poland’s Ministry of Climate and Environment has announced a $257.9 million (PLN 1 billion) subsidy scheme for home battery and heat storage, aimed at increasing self-consumption from residential solar and other renewable energy installations.
The program is open to individuals with grid-connected home solar or other small renewable electricity systems. It will subsidize batteries with at least 10 kWh of capacity and heat storage tanks holding at least 100 liters. Batteries must provide at least 2 kWh of storage per kWp of the accompanying solar installation.
The scheme will cover the costs of purchasing and installing home storage systems. Battery grants will cover up to 30% of eligible costs, capped at approximately $206 (PLN 800) per kWh. Prosumers in the net-billing system can receive up to approximately $4,126 (PLN 16,000), while those in the net-metering system can receive up to approximately $2,063 (PLN 8,000).
Applicants can receive up to 30% of eligible costs for EU-manufactured heat storage systems, capped at approximately $258 (PLN 1,000). An additional bonus of up to approximately $516 (PLN 2,000) is available for an EU-manufactured battery or a necessary replacement EU-manufactured hybrid inverter. Total support is capped at approximately $4,900 (PLN 19,000) per electricity supply point.
The scheme is financed through the Modernization Fund. Applications will open on October 20 and close on October 1, 2027, or when funds are exhausted.
Poland’s Minister of Climate and Environment, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said equipping residential solar installations with energy storage is a ministerial priority.
“The program has two main goals: increasing the efficiency of renewable energy use and strengthening energy security,” she added.
According to the ministry, the number of home energy storage systems in Poland rose from more than 10,000 in the first quarter of 2024 to around 150,000 in June 2026, supported by subsidies and market growth.
The ministry is targeting more than 200,000 home storage systems by the end of 2027.
Sławomir Ćwik, deputy minister of climate and environment, said eligible battery installations must include an energy management system and backup power capability.
“This allows households to maintain power even during grid outages,” Ćwik said.
An initial phase of support financed through Poland’s National Recovery Plan allocated approximately $28.9 million (PLN 112 million) to support the installation of more than 5,000 home battery systems, according to the ministry.
Poland’s Agency for Restructuring and Modernization of Agriculture recently announced a
renewable energy subsidy scheme
aimed at farmers. It opened for applications on October 5.
Following Australia
In Australia, the
Federal government similarly offered a 30% subsidy on home installations of residential batteries
, without a monetary or kWh cap, or need for existing solar installation, though some restrictions were added to cap the total installation sizing.
The scheme has been budgeted to approximately AU$7.2 billion (US$4.68 billion or PLN 18.15 billion), and has seen more than 500,000 households add storage, or some 13 to 14 GWh of behind-the-meter storage capacity.

title: Heliene launches all-black solar module for residential rooftops - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The North American module manufacturer has introduced its 108HC M10 SL All-Black residential solar panel, offering power outputs up to 410 W and 21.0% efficiency built on a 108 half-cut cell architecture.
Ryan Kennedy
06 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
The 108HC M10 SL All-Black solar module
Solar module manufacturer Heliene, Inc. has announced the release of its
108HC M10 SL All-Black solar module
, engineered specifically for residential rooftop applications.
The new framed glass-backsheet panel features 108 half-cut monocrystalline PERC cells based on the M10 wafer format, delivering peak power ratings ranging from 380 W to 410 W with a maximum module efficiency of 21.0%.
The module utilizes split junction box technology to minimize cell-to-module losses and improve thermal management. Constructed with 3.2 mm low-iron, high-transmission solar glass featuring an anti-reflective coating, the panel is built into a 35 mm double-webbed anodized aluminum alloy frame.
The panel measures 1,722 mm by 1,134 mm by 35 mm and weighs 21.5 kg. Electrical performance under standard test conditions ranges from 19.46% to 21.00% efficiency, with a maximum system voltage rating of 1,000 V and a 30 A maximum series fuse rating. For mechanical durability, the module is rated for a 5,400 Pa front load and 2,400 Pa back load, while offering hail resistance capable of withstanding impacts up to 55 mm.
The IP-68 rated junction box houses three bypass diodes and comes equipped with standard 1.2-meter symmetrical 12 AWG cables featuring Stäubli MC4 connectors.
The module is certified under UL 61215, UL 61730, and CSA C22.2 standards, with a Type 1 fire rating. Heliene backs the 108HC M10 SL All-Black with a 25-year product warranty and a 25-year linear performance guarantee covering a maximum first-year power degradation of 2.0% followed by an annual degradation rate of 0.5%, guaranteeing at least 86% of original nameplate output at year 25.
