title: Spacebound silicon - pv magazine Global
content: With excursions into space becoming more frequent, and the reasons behind them more commercial, the industry is exploring ways to generate electricity in space at lower cost and larger scale. And these requirements make ‘terrestrial’ silicon PV technology difficult to ignore. US-based company Source Energy combines commercial silicon cells with a range of module technologies that “makes them suitable for a space environment,” explained Walter Magiera, VP Sales & Marketing at Source. The company has supplied modules to several spacecraft manufacturers, including Impulse Space’s LEO Express 1 that launched in November 2023. It is now working to automate and scale up production at its base in Longmont, Colorado. Among the technologies it has implemented is the shingle-matrix stringer developed by Germany’s M10 Solar Technologies and Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE). Fraunhofer ISE’s Najwa Abdel Latif noted that this technology, where cells are cut into strips and laid out in offset pattern, is particularly well suited to space applications thanks to its “resilience to localized physical damage from impacts by small objects in space, flexibility in layout, and tolerance to extreme temperature differences.” The cell strips are interconnected and bonded using an adhesive, encapsulated between thin glass layers. The resulting product is a compact solar module measuring 321mm x 209mm and weighing 64 grams. Prototypes developed by Source and Fraunhofer ISE reached an average output of 15.6 W and 18.8% efficiency, measured based on outer space irradiance conditions (AM 0). Magiera expects the production line in Colorado to be running at 10 MW annual capacity by the end of this year, increasing to 30 MW by mid-2027. And he notes if customer demand is sufficient, the line can reach a maximum capacity of 100 MW per year. He estimated that at its current scale, the company can deliver modules between $5 and $8/W, depending on volume and other factors. And the company is targeting to get this down to under $3/W, which Magiera expects it to achieve through scale and increasing automation of processes. “We see that as a competitive price. Others in the market are endeavouring to get to $5 or less. It’s all going to come down to manufacturing efficiency and supply chain costs,” said Magiera. He further noted that while silicon modules and arrays are Source Energy’s current products, Heterojunction and copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) thin film are both in development and offer distinct advantages for space deployment.  SOURCE is also tracking tandem perovskites, though the technology will need a mature supply chain before it’s viable for space applications, similar to the trajectory perovskites are following in terrestrial PV. Manufacturing at standard configurations is also key to keeping the costs down and ensuring “off the shelf” availability for customers, as well as assurances that come with extensive testing and qualification of the standard devices. Magiera also stated that it designs its arrays to fit within SpaceX rocket fairing dimensions, the current standard for the majority of launches, and offers those arrays in standard widths to achieve standard power classes and configurations. The same approach extends to other launch vehicles, current and emerging, so arrays adapt to a customer’s platform and power needs rather than being locked to one. The product lineup does offer some flexibility on the configuration, and Magiera also confirmed that Source would accept orders for “bespoke” designs at the right volume. Harsh environment The modules are put through a barrage of tests to ensure they can stand up to the radiation, rapid temperature shifts and other harsh conditions outside of Earth’s atmosphere. Magiera explained that Source has put its standard module designs through 1,500 cycles: -110 C to 90 C + and 40,000 thermal cycles from -70 C to 80 C, as well as proton and electron radiation exposure, designed to be representative of seven years in lower Earth orbit (LEO). “There’s a whole suite of testing that we do to get us to meet the rigours of space,” said Magiera. Fraunhofer ISE testing confirms that Source’s PV modules and arrays can be expected to deliver 76% of their initial output after seven years in space. The research institute also noted that the modules were exposed separately to each stress mechanism, and the result calculated by multiplying the percentage of performance retained after each test. ISE also noted in its results that backing up the results with in-situ testing of modules in space is not currently feasible. However, Magiera said that customers who have already launched SOURCE’s modules have voluntarily shared performance data, and the modules are performing as expected. Developing market Most of the inquiries Source Energy receives today come from customers looking to power satellite telecommunication constellations, as well as various types of Earth observation, and the defence industry. Magiera says the company has also received inquiries regarding data centers in space, but notes a widely held view that launch costs need to fall significantly from their current level of around $7000/kg for that market to take off. Some other applications in space will still need the higher power and long track record of III-V, and be willing to pay a premium for that. But the number of applications for PV in space is growing beyond what the supply chain for those materials, and silicon PV is proving a viable solution for a growing number of companies and missions that need to get to orbit quickly and cost-effectively. title: Indian startup claims over 1,500 cycles for sodium-ion cell with Prussian white cathode - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Indian startup Macsen Energy claims its Prussian white-based sodium-ion battery cell has exceeded 1,500 charge-discharge cycles in laboratory testing, retaining 90% of its initial capacity after 1,000 cycles. The company also plans to build a cathode material production facility and battery cell pilot line, with construction set to begin in 2027.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Prussian white is a sodium-rich cathode material used in sodium-ion batteries.
India-based Macsen Energy Private Limited has announced that a sodium-ion battery cell using its proprietary Prussian white cathode material exceeded 1,500 charge-discharge cycles in laboratory testing. The company did not disclose whether the results had been independently verified by a third party.
“Crossing 1,500 cycles with sustained capacity and high coulombic efficiency, and retaining 90% of the cell’s initial capacity at 1,000 cycles, is an important result for our team,” said Achal Agrawal, CEO of Macsen Group, who is also involved in the research project. “This result comes from cycling an actual sodium-ion cell in our battery research lab. It validates the promise of our cell technology for long-life energy storage and supports the potential of our Prussian White cathode material to deliver sustained performance over repeated cycles.”
Prussian white is a sodium-rich, iron-based compound used as a cathode material in sodium-ion batteries. Its open crystal structure enables the reversible insertion and extraction of sodium ions during charging and discharging. The material offers potential advantages, including low production costs, abundant raw materials, fast charging and long cycle life. Its high sodium content can also support higher initial capacity and energy density.
“Prussian White may appear straightforward to synthesize, but producing a material that approaches its theoretical capacity and maintains strong electrochemical performance over repeated charge-discharge cycles is a much more demanding task,” Agrawal said. “We see it as an engineered battery material, and our work spans chemical synthesis, material characterization, cell fabrication and testing.”
According to its website, Macsen Energy’s primary cell-development approach combines a Prussian white cathode with a hard carbon anode, although it is also investigating alternative anode materials and anode-free configurations. The company lists an operating voltage range of 2.2 V to 4.0 V and an average discharge voltage of approximately 2.5 V to 3.6 V for its cathode material.
The company claims its production process addresses key manufacturing challenges, including moisture sensitivity, oxygen exposure and scalability, while yielding a highly crystalline, fully sodiated material with low water content and improved air stability. It reports a specific capacity exceeding 150 mAh/g, coulombic efficiency of approximately 99.9% and capacity retention of at least 90% after 1,000 charge-discharge cycles. It attributes the material’s performance to its open crystal structure, which enables rapid, reversible sodium-ion movement with minimal structural changes.
Macsen Energy has allocated 10,000 m2 of land for a facility to scale up Prussian blue analogue cathode material production to tonne-scale capacity. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, although the company has not disclosed the location. The site will also house a sodium-ion battery pilot line to further develop Prussian white-based cells, including electrode preparation, cell assembly, validation and performance testing under near-commercial manufacturing conditions.
The company has also initiated research and development into hard carbon synthesis to advance its full-cell technology.

title: Thailand tightens solar panel safety standards - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Thailand will now require crystalline silicon solar panels to meet national safety standards in its latest effort to improve the quality and safety of solar installations.
Patrick Jowett
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Lalida Periswiwatana
The Cabinet of Thailand has approved a draft ministerial regulation requiring crystalline silicon solar panels to comply with the Thai Industrial Standard (TIS), the country’s official national standards organisation.
The TIS enforces product quality and safety rules designed to prevent risks of electric shock, leakage, heat buildup and fire, according to a government press release.
The draft regulation, brought forward by Thailand’s Ministry of Industry, will also require manufacturers or importers of solar panels to obtain a license in accordance with the country’s Industrial Product Standards Act, which regulates national standardisation product quality and safety. It also stipulates distributors can only sell licensed products that meet the TIS, in a bid to prevent the production or import of substandard solar panels.
The regulation is set to come into effect the day following its publication in Thailand’s Royal Gazette.
Government ministers have stated the new standards will not add steps, costs, or delay to the import of solar panels.
The Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) has confirmed that if imported solar products meet International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards, the IEC test results can be submitted to the institute for registration under the TIS without requiring further product inspection or testing. The process takes no more than five days, TISI says.
TISI adds that it is preparing to issue 279 import licenses for solar panels that meet IEC standards this month.
The Ministry of Industry says it plans to gradually review relevant standards covering other solar energy system components, such as inverters, cables, and batteries, before presenting them to the Cabinet “in due course, in order to progressively upgrade the safety standards of solar systems.”
The new regulation is the latest in a series of efforts in Thailand to improve the safety of solar panel installations.
In May, the country’s Office of the Consumer Protection Board
opened an investigation
into substandard solar system installations following growing reports of faulty PV equipment, including signs of melting and burning.
In August, authorities began to
officially register
certified solar installations and PV equipment. The registration forms part of preparations to expand rooftop solar installations in Thailand. The government is currently preparing a two-phase THB 200 billion ($6 billion) energy transition program, with the first phase targeting rooftop solar deployment covering up to 500,000 households.
In the latest update, Lalida Periswiwatana, Deputy Spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, said that while the government is promoting greater public access to solar energy, “the expansion of solar rooftop systems must be coupled with safety measures.”
“The panels installed by the public must be of high quality and meet standards so that people can confidently and safely generate their own electricity, reducing their energy costs,” Periswiwatana added.
Thailand’s cumulative solar capacity reached 6,842 MW at the end of 2025, according to figures from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), compared to 3,388 MW at the end of 2024.

title: What’s driving Europe’s battery boom? Insights from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey and Storage Report - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Europe’s battery storage market is projected to nearly double from 34 GWh in 2025 to 65 GWh in 2026, driven primarily by utility-scale projects and growing renewable energy integration.
Meanwhile, intensifying competition in residential and commercial storage is pushing manufacturers toward integrated energy solutions, strategic partnerships, and advanced energy management technologies.
EUPD Research
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Europe’s battery storage market is entering a new phase as utility-scale projects become the industry’s main growth engine, creating fresh opportunities for manufacturers while reshaping competition across residential and commercial markets. According to EUPD Research’s new calculations, Europe’s (
EU + UK + Switzerland + Norway + Ukraine)
annual battery storage installations are projected to increase from 34 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025 to 65 GWh in 2026, marking one of the region’s fastest periods of market expansion.
The shift reflects more than stronger battery demand. Higher electricity prices, tighter energy markets, expanding renewable generation and supportive policy measures are changing storage from a complementary technology into an increasingly important part of Europe’s electricity system. Rather than serving only as a backup solution for homes and businesses, batteries are becoming a critical tool for balancing power systems as solar and wind account for a larger share of electricity generation.
Recent findings from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey, indicate buoyant demand sentiment across major European markets. The survey gathered responses from a broad base of installation companies, providing a representative view of current market sentiment.
Figure 1: Solar & Storage Demand Across Major European Markets
Utility-Scale Projects Drive the Next Wave of Growth
The strongest momentum is emerging in large-scale battery projects connected directly to the grid. EUPD Research expects the utility segment alone to install a record of around 44 GWh of storage in 2026, making it the largest contributor to Europe’s overall market growth.
Countries with rapidly expanding renewable fleets are leading that transition as grid operators increasingly rely on batteries to shift electricity across different hours of the day, improve system flexibility and support network stability. While electricity prices have eased from the extraordinary peaks seen during Europe’s energy crisis, they remain high enough in many markets to strengthen the business case for storage investments.
Policy is reinforcing that trend. European electricity market reforms, funding mechanisms, permitting improvements and national storage support measures are creating a more favorable environment for deployment, particularly for larger projects that help integrate growing volumes of renewable electricity. At the same time, changing incentive structures in several countries are encouraging households and businesses to maximize self-consumption, making batteries more attractive as export payments for rooftop solar decline or net-metering schemes begin to phase out.
Bigger Projects Reshape the Competitive Landscape
The expansion of utility-scale storage is changing how manufacturers participate in Europe’s battery storage market. As projects become larger and more complex, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies are becoming increasingly specialized, creating a more structured project ecosystem than the fragmented market that characterized earlier stages of deployment.
Insights from the newly released
EUPD PV and Storage C&I EPCMonitor
indicate that local contractors continue serving smaller installations, while national leaders, regional players and pan-European firms are taking on progressively larger battery projects across multiple countries. That differentiation is creating multiple routes to market for manufacturers, allowing suppliers to build longer-term partnerships with contractors that specialize in infrastructure-scale delivery instead of relying primarily on equipment sales.
Project size is increasingly defining competitive positioning. Companies focused on smaller systems continue serving distributed markets, while firms capable of delivering larger projects are becoming more important as utilities, developers and industrial customers pursue higher-capacity installations. The result is a market where partnerships and delivery capabilities are becoming as important as battery technology itself.
Figure 2: Annual Installed EES Capacity | Company Type | 2025
Residential Storage Enters a More Competitive Phase
While utility-scale deployment is accelerating, distributed storage is entering a more mature stage rather than slowing. Europe’s residential market is becoming increasingly sophisticated as manufacturers expand beyond standalone batteries into broader home-energy ecosystems that combine rooftop solar, electric vehicle charging, heat pumps, energy management software and grid-flexibility services.
Several market forces continue supporting residential adoption. High retail electricity prices, declining battery costs, tax incentives, value-added tax (VAT) exemptions and growing interest in energy independence remain important drivers across Europe. However, the market also faces persistent challenges, including uneven smart-meter deployment, financing constraints, labor shortages and the gradual reduction of some subsidy programs in certain countries.
Despite those headwinds, EUPD Research expects Europe to install roughly 15 GWh of new residential battery capacity during 2026, with Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and the United Kingdom remaining among the strongest-performing markets.
According to EUPD Research’s latest
EES Report Europe
, the competitive landscape is evolving just as quickly as deployment. Residential supplier rankings have already shifted between 2025 and the first half of 2026, illustrating how rapidly manufacturers are competing for market share as customer preferences change. Germany’s residential storage market is becoming increasingly fragmented, as share gradually shifts away from the leading suppliers. The top suppliers’ combined share declined between 2025 and H1 2026, while mid-sized brands and smaller brands expanded their presence. These trends point to a market where competition is intensifying and leadership positions are becoming less secure.
Figure 3: Germany’s Residential Storage Supplier Landscape: 2025 Vs H1 2026
Instead of competing only on battery hardware, manufacturers are increasingly differentiating themselves through integrated energy solutions, software capabilities and broader customer offerings that create additional value after installation.
Storage Becomes Core Energy Infrastructure
Europe’s battery market is increasingly developing along two complementary paths rather than replacing one segment with another. Utility-scale batteries are becoming essential infrastructure for balancing renewable electricity and supporting grid operations, while distributed storage is expanding its role within homes and businesses through integrated energy-management systems.
For manufacturers, this creates a dual opportunity. Larger grid-connected projects provide access to infrastructure-scale investment, while distributed markets offer opportunities to deepen customer relationships through broader energy solutions and connected technologies. As Europe moves toward a projected 65 GWh storage market in 2026, batteries are becoming less of a standalone clean-energy product and more of a core component of the region’s evolving electricity system.
The next phase of this market will be shaped not only by how many batteries are installed, but also by how effectively storage becomes embedded across both the power grid and the wider energy ecosystem. Partnerships and delivery capabilities will become increasingly important, particularly in the commercial and industrial segment, where solar, storage and energy management are converging into a single business case.
This is where industry collaboration becomes critical. European Sustainability Week 2026, taking place from 23 to 25 November at the historic Petersberg near Bonn, brings together manufacturers, EPCs, utilities, investors and industrial energy buyers to explore these developments. As Europe’s C&I event for sustainable industries, with a clear focus on renewable energy, solar and storage, it provides a platform for the exchange of market insights and practical solutions. At the Environmental Forum on 24 November, EUPD Research will share the latest market insights, while industry leaders will discuss how storage can become core infrastructure for European businesses.
Last year, more than 600 decision-makers from over 23 countries took part. Registration is open at

title: Spain and Portugal record Europe’s highest number of hours with negative electricity prices in Q2 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Spain and Portugal recorded the highest number of hours with negative electricity prices in Europe in the second quarter of 2026, according to Montel’s European Power Market Outlook Q3 2026 report. The period was marked by record solar power generation, a heatwave in late June and significant electricity price volatility.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
European solar power generation exceeded the previous record by nearly 20%, supported by prolonged periods of high pressure and abundant sunshine. The increase in output led to recurring electricity surpluses around midday, pushing intraday prices to record negative levels in several markets.
The distribution of negative-price periods also shifted compared with the previous year. Spain recorded the highest number of hours with negative electricity prices, at 596, followed by Portugal with 462, France with 370 and Greece with 317. By contrast, Nordic markets experienced fewer such periods. The report attributes these differences to variations in solar capacity growth and electricity demand patterns across Europe.
In Spain, daily and weekly electricity prices repeatedly exceeded €100 ($112.3)/MWh during the late-June heatwave, following a period of high renewable power generation and negative midday prices. In Germany, electricity prices surged above €600/MWh during evening peak hours.
These developments highlighted contrasting market conditions. While high solar output created electricity surpluses during certain hours, rising demand during periods of extreme heat pushed prices higher during peak consumption periods. According to Montel, these fluctuations exposed the limitations of flexibility resources available to European electricity markets.
In late April, prices in some European markets approached the technical floor of €-500/MWh, which was subsequently lowered to €-600/MWh.
Flexible resources shift away from day-ahead markets
The report also identifies a gradual withdrawal of certain flexible resources from day-ahead electricity markets. In response to recurring negative prices, some flexible thermal power plants, storage operators and industrial consumers opted against submitting bids at negative price levels in day-ahead auctions, instead reserving their capacity for intraday or balancing markets.
According to Montel, this shift could move more system-balancing activity into intraday markets, potentially increasing price volatility. It could also increase the value of flexible resources capable of responding rapidly to fluctuations in electricity generation and demand.
The report highlights grid reinforcement, more granular bidding zones, and faster curtailment and redispatch mechanisms as key measures for managing cross-border electricity flows and local grid congestion.
The extreme price fluctuations observed in the second quarter illustrate the growing challenges facing European electricity markets as solar capacity expands. Periods of surplus generation and negative prices increasingly coincide with sharp price spikes during high-demand hours, underscoring the need for greater system flexibility.

title: Black Death to smallpox: 7 deadly plagues that reshaped societies
content: Long before scientists could identify bacteria or sequence viruses, infectious diseases traveled with soldiers, merchants, and ships. While some outbreaks overwhelmed cities within months, others spread across continents and continued killing for generations.The deadliest plagues in history reveal how closely disease follows human movement. They also show why comparing death tolls is difficult: ancient records are incomplete, estimates vary, and some pandemics remain ongoing.These seven events are presented without a strict ranking because their durations and death estimates differ considerably.1. Black DeathThe Black Death swept through Europe during the mid-14th century, devastating communities and disrupting trade, farming, and everyday life. Widely cited estimates place death toll across affected regions between 75 million and 200 million, although the true total remains uncertain. The disease was caused by Yersinia pestis, the bacterium responsible for plague.Modern researchers have traced part of its history through DNA preserved in human remains. A 2022 study recovered plague genomes from burials dated to 1338 and 1339 in present-day Kyrgyzstan. The findings linked those infections to the bacterial lineage behind the Black Death, providing evidence of its origins in Central Asia.2. The 1918 influenza pandemicThe 1918 influenza pandemic infected an estimated one-third of the world’s population and killed at least 50 million people, including approximately 675,000 in the United States. Although commonly called the Spanish flu, its geographical origin remains unresolved. One particularly striking feature was its high mortality among otherwise healthy adults aged 20–40.The virus spread during World War I, when troop movements and crowded living conditions helped carry infections between communities. Doctors lacked influenza vaccines and antibiotics to treat secondary bacterial infections. Decades later, scientists recovered genetic material from preserved tissues and reconstructed the virus under tightly controlled laboratory conditions to investigate what made it so dangerous.3. The HIV/AIDS pandemicFirst recognized in 1981, the HIV/AIDS pandemic developed over decades rather than as a single, short outbreak. WHO estimates available for 2024 put cumulative deaths from HIV-related causes at approximately 44.1 million since the epidemic began. That total reflects a continuing global burden, with the WHO African Region remaining the most severely affected.HIV attacks the immune system, leaving untreated individuals vulnerable to serious infections and certain cancers. Antiretroviral therapy changed that outlook by suppressing the virus and protecting immune function. 4. The COVID-19 pandemicCOVID-19 emerged in late 2019 and spread internationally within months. Its death toll illustrates how much the method of counting matters. WHO estimated approximately 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the pandemic during 2020 and 2021 alone, substantially exceeding the deaths officially reported as directly caused by COVID-19 during that period.Excess mortality compares the number of people who died with the number expected without the crisis. It captures both direct deaths and indirect losses, including those associated with disrupted healthcare. The estimate is therefore neither a count of laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 deaths nor the pandemic’s complete lifetime toll. It provides a broader measure of its impact during those two years.5. The Justinianic plagueThe Justinianic plague reached Constantinople in 541, during the reign of Byzantine Emperor Justinian I. Historical accounts describe a severe outbreak that overwhelmed the city.Popular summaries frequently cite tens of millions of deaths, but researchers continue to debate how extensive the mortality was and how strongly the pandemic affected the wider Mediterranean world.Scientific evidence has identified Yersinia pestis as the pathogen involved. Establishing the bacterium’s presence, however, does not establish a precise death toll. Researchers examining historical and environmental evidence have challenged sweeping claims about population collapse. 6. The third plague pandemicThe third plague pandemic began in southwestern China in 1855 and spread worldwide, reaching ports and inland communities across inhabited continents.A University of St Andrews research project places its death toll at approximately 12 million through 1959. International shipping helped connect outbreaks in widely separated places.This pandemic also brought a major scientific breakthrough. Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium in 1894 during the Hong Kong outbreak. Understanding the pathogen and its transmission through infected fleas helped turn an apparently mysterious catastrophe into a disease that could be investigated and controlled. 7. Smallpox epidemics in the AmericasSmallpox devastated Indigenous communities following European arrival in the Americas. An outbreak reached present-day Mexico in 1520, followed by repeated waves of disease. Communities with no previous exposure to the virus suffered catastrophic losses, while other introduced infections, including measles and influenza, compounded the destruction.The death toll requires particular care. Large estimates for Indigenous population decline encompass multiple diseases and the wider effects of colonization, rather than smallpox alone. Presenting those losses as one smallpox outbreak creates a misleading comparison. This was a succession of epidemics across different regions and decades, whose combined consequences reshaped societies throughout the Americas.What these outbreaks revealThese outbreaks differed in their pathogens, transmission routes, and duration. Their histories also reflect the changing tools available to study disease, from written observations to laboratory testing and ancient DNA.Death estimates help convey their scale, but understanding how those figures were produced matters just as much. A precise-looking number can conceal incomplete records, disputed assumptions, or several different causes of death.

title: How material shortages crushed Nazi Germany’s 1945 nuclear program
content: When the American forces in 1945 reached Nazi Germany’s final experimental nuclear reactor, the B8 pile, they found a machine that had never sustained a nuclear chain reaction.They dismantled it, but a question lingered: how close had the Germans come to making it work?Werner Heisenberg, the project’s scientific leader, later described the B8 pile as just short of success. Decades later, two surviving uranium cubes and a trail of wartime documents gave researchers a way to test that claim.Timothy Koeth and his colleagues found a much larger obstacle than Heisenberg’s account suggested. The reactor needed about twice the uranium it contained, and roughly twice the heavy water its Norwegian supplier produced during the entire war.How the B8 reactor was supposed to workThe B8 pile used natural uranium as fuel and heavy water as a neutron moderator. Both materials played distinct roles in the attempt to sustain nuclear fission.When a uranium atom splits, it releases neutrons that can cause other uranium atoms to split. A reactor reaches criticality when enough of those neutrons trigger further fissions to maintain a chain reaction without it dying out.However, neutrons released during fission move too quickly to efficiently sustain that process in the German design. The moderator slows them down, increasing their ability to cause additional fissions.German scientists selected heavy water, which contains deuterium, a heavier isotope of hydrogen. Having uranium alone was therefore insufficient. The reactor also required enough moderator to support the chain reaction.Why the material shortage matteredKoeth and his colleagues examined two natural uranium cubes from Germany’s wartime nuclear program alongside historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and other archival sources.Their reconstruction indicated that reaching criticality required about twice the uranium already present in the B8 pile. The heavy water requirement presented an even greater obstacle: it amounted to roughly twice Norsk Hydro’s entire wartime production.The Norwegian facility at Vemork was Germany’s source of heavy water, making the reactor program dependent on a limited supply that Allied operations repeatedly targeted.Graphite offered no practical escape from that shortage. Although it can moderate neutrons in some reactors, the researchers found that graphite available in German-controlled areas was unsuitable for this purpose.What this reveals about Germany’s nuclear ambitionsThe distinction between a reactor approaching criticality and one requiring vastly greater material supplies changes how the B8 experiment should be understood.Heisenberg’s account suggested a relatively narrow gap between failure and success. The analysis instead identifies shortages that could not be overcome through adjustments to the existing machine alone.A working reactor also would not, by itself, have constituted a nuclear weapon. Reactors represented one possible route to producing fissile material for a bomb, which helped make Germany’s progress a concern for the Manhattan Project.The B8 findings address that earlier milestone. According to the researchers’ assessment, Germany lacked the uranium and suitable moderator needed to make its final reactor design sustain a chain reaction.

title: New MK 82 Penetrator is built to punch through 3.2-foot concrete
content: The United Arab Emirates has completed development of an aircraft munition designed to penetrate hardened targets, with its manufacturer reporting that the weapon can breach more than one meter of reinforced concrete during testing.Developed and manufactured by LAHAB, a munitions subsidiary of Emirati defense group EDGE, the MK 82 Penetrator is intended for attacking fortified positions and bunkers. The weapon builds on the familiar MK 82 general-purpose bomb format, allowing operators to add a hardened-target capability without introducing an entirely separate aircraft-weapons system.A new role for a familiar aircraft munitionAccording to EDGE, the development program concluded with performance trials against multiple hardened target types and environmental qualification testing. The company said the munition penetrated reinforced concrete more than one meter thick while avoiding what it calls the “J” effect, in which a weapon deviates from its intended trajectory during impact.The reported result suggests that the weapon is designed to maintain a more consistent path through a hardened structure. However, EDGE has not publicly detailed the full test conditions, including the concrete’s precise composition, the impact velocity, or the munition’s performance against different types of fortified structures. The published penetration figure should therefore be understood as a manufacturer-reported test result rather than a universal measure of battlefield performance.LAHAB CEO Mohammed Arbabi said the weapon was developed to expand customer capabilities while retaining familiarity and ease of use. The company has positioned the MK 82 Penetrator as an option for hardened, reinforced targets and bunkers.The weapon’s compatibility with existing aircraft and guidance equipment is another central part of its design.Designed to work with existing aircraft and guidance kitsEDGE says the MK 82 Penetrator is compatible with NATO-configuration aircraft across several generations, including fourth- and 4.5-generation multirole fighters, variable-geometry strike aircraft, advanced jet trainers and light attack platforms. The company also lists fifth-generation fighters, subject to the relevant aircraft’s existing compatibility and clearance for MK 82 weapons.The munition can be paired with precision-guidance kits from EDGE’s AL TARIQ and THUNDER families. These systems are designed to provide guidance capabilities to compatible aircraft weapons, giving operators a way to combine precision guidance with the new penetrator variant.That approach could reduce the need to introduce a completely separate guidance architecture for customers already using compatible weapons and aircraft. Actual integration, however, depends on the aircraft configuration, weapon certification and the guidance kit selected.A larger penetrator is already in developmentThe MK 82 is the first of two planned penetrator variants. EDGE says development of the larger MK 83 Penetrator has reached an advanced stage, although it has not disclosed a completion date or detailed performance specifications for the new variant.The program also fits into the UAE’s more comprehensive effort to develop and manufacture more defense equipment domestically. Building local expertise in munition design, testing and qualification can give the country greater control over production and support while creating products for potential export customers.EDGE has announced the reported concrete-penetration result and aircraft compatibility, but has not publicly provided detailed independent test data or disclosed which armed forces will field the weapon first. The planned MK 83 variant suggests the company intends to extend the concept beyond a single munition, creating a broader family of weapons for targets protected by reinforced structures.

title: China pulls oil from 19,685-feet below at its largest desert oilfield
content: China’s largest desert oilfield has crossed a major production milestone after extracting more than 26 million metric tons (29.6 million U.S. tons) of oil and gas from formations buried deeper than 6,000 meters (19,685 feet) beneath the Taklimakan Desert.China National Petroleum Corp. (CNPC), which operates the Fuman Oilfield in the Tarim Basin, announced the milestone on Monday. The development highlights the growing push to tap ultra-deep hydrocarbon resources in one of China’s most challenging oil-producing regions.Core recovered from 26,509 feetThe latest breakthrough came at the Zhentan-1 well near the edge of the Taklimakan Desert. Engineers recently recovered rock cores from a depth of 8,080 meters (26,509 feet), providing samples of formations buried for about 500 million years.It is the first time China has retrieved a core sample from deeper than 8,000 meters (26,247 feet) in the northwestern part of the Tarim Basin.The Taklimakan Desert occupies much of the Tarim Basin in southern Xinjiang. The basin contains extensive sedimentary formations that have become a major target for China’s ultra-deep oil and gas exploration.“With these precious rock cores, we can analyze and evaluate the hydrocarbon generation potential below 8,000 meters, including the thickness of the oil and gas layers and their maturity levels,” Xu Yanan, director of the Tarim Oilfield project at CNPC, as reported by the China Central Television (CCTV) News.More than 29 million tons producedThe Fuman Oilfield has now produced substantial volumes from its ultra-deep formations. According to CNPC figures reported by CCTV, the operation has extracted 20.36 million metric tons (22.4 million tons) of crude oil and 8.15 billion cubic meters (287.8 billion cubic feet) of natural gas.“We have already extracted 20.36 million tons of crude oil and 8.15 billion cubic meters of natural gas from the ultra-deep formations beneath the Taklimakan Desert, with a combined oil and gas equivalent exceeding 26.86 million tons,” said Lu Zhongyuan, an engineer at CNPC’s Tarim Oilfield, according to CCTV report.485 wells reach extreme depthsCNPC has expanded drilling across the Fuman Oilfield as it seeks to unlock more resources beneath the desert. A total of 485 ultra-deep wells have now been drilled at the field.Of these wells, 133 have each produced more than 100,000 metric tons (more than 110,000 tons) of oil and gas. Another 464 wells have each exceeded 10,000 metric tons (more than 11,000 tons) of cumulative production.The scale of production has helped establish the Tarim Oilfield as China’s largest desert oilfield and a major base for ultra-deep hydrocarbon production.Tarim holds vast deep reservesThe latest drilling results could help researchers better understand hydrocarbon resources located several miles beneath the surface. The recovered cores will provide geological information about formations that are difficult to study using conventional exploration methods.The Tarim Basin is already an important source of China’s oil and gas reserves. The basin has more than 5 billion metric tons (more than 5.5 billion tons) of proven oil and gas reserves, with more than half located in ultra-deep formations below 6,000 meters (19,685 feet).As production moves deeper beneath the Taklimakan Desert, these formations are becoming increasingly important to China’s efforts to expand domestic hydrocarbon reserves and output.

title: Carbon blocks to store heat in 5.8 GWh US thermal battery project
content: A Kansas ethanol producer is preparing to use a nearly 6 gigawatt-hour thermal battery system to supply its plant with energy around the clock. Antora Energy announced the 5.8 GWh project on October 1 for Pratt Energy’s biorefinery in Pratt.The planned installation stores energy for multiple days and is intended to provide affordable, reliable energy for the facility. Antora describes it as one of the world’s largest battery storage systems once completed.Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners led the project’s third-party equity financing through its credit platform, with Grok Ventures and University Pension Plan Ontario also participating. The announcement connects the investment to industrial energy demand and economic development in the Kansas community.Turning electricity into stored heatThe system uses insulated blocks of solid carbon to hold energy as heat. Electricity charges the thermal batteries, and the stored heat can subsequently serve industrial processes. Antora’s technology can also deliver power.At Pratt Energy, the commercial arrangement is a long-term heat offtake agreement. Energy deliveries are scheduled to start in 2027, giving the biorefinery access to an around-the-clock supply.The Kansas project follows Antora’s commissioning of a 5 GWh system in Big Stone City, South Dakota. That earlier installation has a 50 MW rating; the Pratt announcement does not specify an equivalent power rating.Antora manufactures its batteries in San Jose, California. An expansion earlier in 2026 added two facilities and doubled the site’s manufacturing capacity. The Pratt deployment is the company’s second major thermal battery project announced this year.Backing cleaner ethanol productionFor Pratt Energy, the installation supports a broader ambition to produce zero-carbon-intensity ethanol. It represents a step toward that goal, rather than confirmation that the plant has achieved it.The company expects lower-carbon production to create opportunities in additional markets. Reliable energy is also central to its plans to improve the competitiveness of its products.The project’s financing brings together infrastructure and investment firms from several countries. Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ involvement is through its credit platform, while Australian firm Grok Ventures and Canada’s University Pension Plan Ontario joined the equity financing.Antora said the deployment is expected to consume little additional water beyond the plant’s existing needs and operate without raising noise levels at neighboring properties. Those statements describe anticipated operating conditions.Training workers alongside the deploymentThe project is expected to create and support more than 100 construction and operations jobs. Antora also plans to prioritize local candidates for permanent operating positions.“Reliable energy is the foundation of everything we do, and this project lays that foundation for decades to come,” said Pratt Energy CEO Travis Lane.A paid internship program with Pratt Community College has already sent two students to Antora’s South Dakota project. Separately, scholarships administered through the South Central Community Foundation are intended to support up to 12 Pratt students over three years. Antora is also establishing a community impact fund, with grants beginning in 2027 and funding decisions assigned to Pratt County residents.

title: US Navy taps advanced 3D-printed rocket motors for next-gen missiles
content: The US Navy has awarded two contracts worth a combined $137 million to develop solid rocket motors for two new missile programs. The contracts given to Colorado-based aerospace and defense company Ursa Major cover propulsion for a Compact Air-to-Air Missile (CAAM) and the medium-range version of the Naval Modular Missile (NMM).Contracts include funding of $91 million for the CAAM solid rocket motor and $46 million for the NMM Quad-Pack Medium-Range motor.The systems are part of the Navy’s efforts to develop new weapons for fighter aircraft and surface ships. Compact missile motorThe $91 million CAAM contract covers a compact motor for an air-launched missile intended for fighter aircraft and future carrier-based drones. The $46 million NMM contract covers a larger motor for a ship-launched interceptor being developed to eventually replace members of the Navy’s Standard Missile family. The funding comes through the Office of the Under Secretary of War.For CAAM, Ursa Major is developing a 7-inch (178 mm) solid rocket motor. The diameter is similar to that of the AIM-120 AMRAAM and larger than the 5-inch AIM-9X Sidewinder. CAAM is designed as a short-range weapon that can be carried inside the weapons bays of stealth aircraft, allowing them to carry more air-to-air missiles without increasing their external weapons load.The motor uses Ursa Major’s Highly Loaded Grain technology, which increases the amount of propellant packed into the motor case. The approach is intended to provide higher energy within the limited volume available in a compact missile.Ursa Major is also developing the motor using manufacturing methods intended for full-scale production. This could allow the company to transition the design to higher-rate manufacturing after qualification rather than developing a separate production process.“By investing in CAAM and NMM, the Navy and OUSW are building solid rocket motor capacity now and getting new tactical air and naval capabilities into development sooner,” said Jason Meredith, president, Solid Missile Systems at Ursa Major, in a statement.NMM gains rocket motorThe second contract covers a 10-inch (254 mm) solid rocket motor for the medium-range NMM. The motor is designed for high-rate production and compatibility with existing Navy shipboard launch systems.NMM is being developed as a modular naval missile family, with the medium-range version intended to fit four missiles into a single launch cell. This quad-pack configuration is similar to the Navy’s use of the Evolved Sea Sparrow Missile and would allow ships to carry more interceptors within the same launcher capacity.Ursa Major is using its Lynx manufacturing approach for the programs. The process relies heavily on additive manufacturing, or industrial 3D printing, to produce rocket motor components. The company is developing the motors with production scalability in mind as the US seeks to expand domestic solid rocket motor capacity.Solid rocket motor manufacturing has historically been concentrated among a small number of major US suppliers, including Northrop Grumman and L3Harris-owned Aerojet Rocketdyne. The Pentagon has been supporting additional production capacity as demand for missile interceptors and other weapons increases.The new contracts build on Ursa Major’s previous work with the Navy. In July, the service awarded the company $10 million to advance its MK 104 solid rocket motor through critical design review and static-fire testing. The MK 104 powers the Standard Missile-2 and Standard Missile-6 used by Aegis-equipped Navy ships.In February, Ursa Major also completed a $25 million cost-share program with the Navy and the Office of Strategic Capital. The effort involved designing, building, and static-firing a 10-inch Highly Loaded Grain motor and developing a proprietary solid propellant. The work was conducted with the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division at China Lake and the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division.

title: Big tech's nuclear energy plans continue with Google's new deal talks
content: Can nuclear energy satisfy AI’s endless demand for power? It is too early to know for sure, but Alphabet is betting over $1 billion that it can.Reports suggest that Google’s parent company, Alphabet Inc., is nearing a massive multi-year agreement to buy nuclear energy from Constellation Energy Corp. According to sources familiar with the matter, the deal is expected to be valued at $1 billion or more and could be announced as early as this week. It is a striking figure. But in the world of generative AI, where data centers gulp gigawatts like water, a billion dollars is just the cover charge to keep the power running.Rush for uninterrupted powerAI models demand continuous power that renewable sources like solar and wind cannot consistently provide because they depend on the weather. Nuclear energy could supply steady, carbon-free baseload power around the clock. Google’s electricity demand soared from 12.8 terawatt-hours in 2019 to 44 terawatt-hours in 2025. Over 95 per cent of Alphabet’s total global electricity consumption goes directly to its data centers, with administrative offices and corporate campuses accounting for the remaining 5 per cent. The tech giant counters this surge by deploying custom high-performance servers, machine learning, intelligent climate controls, and advanced cooling systems across its data centers. These targeted efficiency measures ensure that hardware operates with minimal energy waste even as global computing loads expand.However, building brand-new nuclear reactors is a slow process. This leaves tech companies with little choice but to squeeze every remaining drop of capacity from existing infrastructure. Alphabet’s potential agreement with Constellation follows a flurry of similar moves across the tech sector. Amazon recently inked a 690-megawatt power agreement with Constellation linked to Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs facility, while Microsoft backed the restart of Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island plant. Google similarly laid groundwork through partnerships with NextEra Energy to reopen Iowa’s Duane Arnold reactor and investments in upgrades at two Southern Co. nuclear sites.The net-zero paradoxHigh costs and safety concerns cooled global enthusiasm for atomic energy. But global attitudes toward it have shifted in recent years. Nations aiming to hit climate targets are aligning with technology firms seeking reliable electricity, driving a widespread revival of nuclear power worldwide.Yet, the huge need for computing power also creates a clear conflict for the company. Alphabet set an ambitious goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions across all operations by 2030, but its latest environmental report highlights an 81 percent surge in greenhouse gas emissions compared to the 2019 baseline.Driven by the rapid growth of AI over the past five years, the company secured over 12 gigawatts of net-new clean energy in 2025 alone. The long-term strategy focuses on advancing next-generation clean sources such as nuclear energy and enhanced geothermal, alongside strategic investments in commercial fusion power.To optimize grid connection timelines, grid software unicorn Emerald AI formed a coalition with Google and Nvidia.Operating as the AI Energy Management Alliance, the group uses Emerald AI’s technology to enable demand response mechanisms that temporarily reduce or shift data center power usage during peak grid stress. The coalition estimates that pausing noncritical tasks and adjusting compute loads could free up capacity for an additional 100 gigawatts of data center infrastructure to connect to the power grid.Neither Google nor Constellation Energy offered official commentary on the reported deal. Specific details regarding the exact output scale and geographic locations of the nuclear capacity remain undisclosed.Nevertheless, the broader trend is clear: accelerating AI workloads could mean permanently binding tech’s growth to the reliability of the nuclear grid.

title: Kawasaki bets on physical AI to make Kaleido humanoid fully autonomous
content: Kawasaki plans to integrate Japanese physical AI developer Noetra’s physical AI platform into its Kaleido humanoid robot.The move would make Kaleido the first planned adopter of Noetra’s physical AI technology, according to Nikkei Asia. Kawasaki is expected to initially use a combination of remote human control and AI as the system develops toward greater autonomy. The company’s plans reflect a gradual expansion of humanoid robots into industrial operations, beginning with relatively simple tasks before potentially moving to more complex work such as assembly and other manufacturing activities.Kawasaki adds AIKawasaki Heavy Industries is set to add Noetra’s platform into its Kaleido humanoid robot, with deployment targeted as early as 2030.Kaleido has been under development since 2015 and is being positioned for industrial applications. Kawasaki’s initial plans focus on relatively simple tasks such as facility patrols and transporting parts in factories and warehouses. The company is also discussing the robot with potential customers in the automotive and semiconductor industries.The transition to autonomous operation is expected to happen in stages. Early deployments would combine remote human control with AI, allowing operators to supervise or control the robot while Noetra’s physical AI capabilities handle an increasing share of tasks. As the underlying AI develops, Kawasaki aims to reduce the need for human intervention and eventually achieve fully autonomous operation, reports Humanoids Daily.The approach reflects a technical challenge facing humanoid robots in industrial settings. Performing a predefined movement in a controlled environment is considerably different from operating autonomously around people, equipment and changing surroundings. A robot needs to perceive its environment, understand the physical properties of objects, plan movements and adjust its actions when conditions change.Kawasaki’s Kaleido 9 already demonstrates some of these capabilities. The company has shown autonomous walking with obstacle avoidance using LiDAR-based localization, as well as remote-operated disaster-rescue demonstrations. Kawasaki’s March 2026 roadmap places remote-assisted work in controlled environments around 2030, while autonomous operation in unstructured environments is targeted around 2040.Kaleido targets autonomyNoetra’s physical AI platform is intended to provide another layer of capability. The company is developing an omni-modal foundation model targeted for fiscal 2028 and physical-world AI capable of understanding physical properties by fiscal 2030. Its technology development involves Sony, SoftBank, NEC and Honda, while Kawasaki is also an investor.For Kaleido, the technology could eventually extend its role beyond basic transportation and patrol work. Kawasaki expects future software and AI improvements to enable more demanding applications, including product assembly. Such tasks require substantially greater precision because the robot must coordinate its arms and hands while responding to objects, tools and workpieces in real time.Kawasaki also plans to combine Noetra’s technology with its physical AI collaboration with NVIDIA. Announced in May, the collaboration is focused on developing more complex and precise autonomous movements. Combining the two efforts could give Kawasaki access to AI models and computing technologies while allowing it to apply them to its existing humanoid platform.The company’s plans also indicate that humanoids are only one part of a broader robotics strategy. Kawasaki is targeting tens of thousands of robots in operation by 2040, including wheeled robots, quadruped machines and hospital transport robots alongside humanoids.The key technical goal for Kaleido is therefore not simply to make the robot perform more tasks, but to gradually shift responsibility for those tasks from human operators to AI. The planned 2030 deployment would represent an early stage of that transition rather than an immediate move to completely autonomous humanoid operation.

title: ML-powered cat search network helps find missing pets
content: Cats are famously good at getting into places humans cannot easily reach. Now, in Kazakhstan, some are putting that talent to work helping find missing pets. A project called GdeKotBot has recruited free-roaming cats as four-legged search volunteers, equipping them with tiny cameras and GPS trackers while artificial intelligence scans their footage for missing animals.The idea builds on a digital service launched in 2025 that uses a Telegram chatbot to connect people who have lost cats with residents who spot them outdoors. The new initiative adds an unusual twist: instead of relying entirely on human volunteers, the search network can also gather footage from cats exploring their neighbourhoods.How AI turns cats into search volunteersAccording to GdeKotBot, the project has helped reunite 407 pets with their owners, while more than 28,000 users have joined the service. The team says the new volunteer-cat initiative is designed to expand the search into places where frightened animals might hide. The figures have been reported by local media, although they have not been independently audited.The system begins when an owner reports a missing pet through the @GdeKotBot Telegram bot, submitting photographs and information about where the animal disappeared. Anyone who encounters a cat outdoors can then upload a photograph and its location. AI compares the submitted image with missing-pet reports and alerts the owner when it identifies a possible match.The volunteer cats extend this process. Owners of free-roaming cats in neighbourhoods with many missing-pet reports are invited to participate. Their pets wear cameras and GPS trackers during their usual outings, recording other cats they encounter. AI analyses the resulting footage and compares the animals against the missing-pet database.If the system finds a potential match, the missing cat’s owner can receive an alert with location information, giving them a lead to follow up on.Why cats can be difficult to findThe approach addresses a familiar problem for pet owners. A missing cat may be nearby without being visible or approachable. Frightened animals often hide under cars, inside bushes, beneath porches or in other sheltered spaces. They may avoid people even when someone is actively searching for them. A cat already roaming the neighbourhood, meanwhile, might pass through some of those same spaces during its normal daily route.That does not make feline volunteers perfect search agents. Their cameras can miss animals, footage may be unclear, and AI image matching can produce false positives. But the extra observations could provide useful clues when combined with photographs and reports submitted by people.The project is also designed to make participation possible without owning a camera-equipped cat. Residents can still help simply by photographing an animal they encounter and sharing the image and location through the chatbot.A local search network with wider ambitionsGdeKotBot began in Almaty, Kazakhstan, in 2025, as a way to coordinate reports of missing and spotted cats. The service’s broader approach includes circulating missing-pet information through local communication channels, helping connect sightings with the area where an animal disappeared.The camera-equipped cats represent an expansion of that community-based model rather than a replacement for it. Their footage adds another source of information, while people remain essential to reporting missing animals, checking potential matches and bringing pets home safely.There are limitations to consider, too. The system depends on participating owners, usable camera footage and accurate image matching. The organisers’ reported reunion figures do not show how much the camera-equipped cats themselves have contributed, separate from the original chatbot and its human users.Still, the concept demonstrates a practical application of AI that goes beyond generating text or images. By combining computer vision, location data and a network of local participants, GdeKotBot is attempting to turn everyday observations into actionable information. And its newest volunteers have an advantage no human search team can easily replicate. They already know their way around the neighbourhood.

title: US taps four firms for directed-energy homeland defense weapons
content: The US Defense Department has selected four companies for a pilot program to test directed-energy weapons for homeland defense. The initiative will examine how high-energy laser and high-powered microwave systems can be used in operational settings against emerging threats. The program is intended to give the military practical experience deploying, integrating, and sustaining these technologies outside laboratory and test environments. The effort comes as the Pentagon explores new approaches to countering threats that could challenge existing defense systems and require faster, more scalable responses.Directed energy trialThe US Defense Department has selected four directed-energy systems for a pilot program aimed at evaluating their use against drone threats in the US homeland.The systems were selected under a requirement in the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. The Army-led Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) will oversee the program and assess the technologies in operational environments.The selected systems are AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser, Epirus’ Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system, Kord’s Firefly High-Energy Laser, and Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon System.The pilot will generate real-world data on the systems’ performance, requirements, costs, and deployment practices. The task force will also examine how the weapons can be integrated with existing counter-unmanned aircraft systems and sustained during operations.“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense. This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland,” said Matt Ross, US Army Brig. Gen. and director of JIATF-401, in a statement.JIATF-401 will work with the Federal Aviation Administration, US Northern Command and the military services as the systems are tested. Coordination with the FAA is particularly important because directed-energy weapons can operate in areas where civilian aircraft share the airspace.US advances counter-droneThe need for such coordination became clear earlier this year after an incident involving a counter-drone laser near El Paso, Texas. The FAA temporarily closed airspace around the airport following a misunderstanding between federal agencies over the use of a laser operated by Customs and Border Protection. The system had been loaned by the Army.Since then, JIATF-401 and the FAA have worked together to establish procedures for safely operating directed-energy systems. The agencies conducted a safety risk assessment during a live-fire high-energy laser demonstration at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico.The FAA determined that the system presented minimal risk to the National Airspace System. The assessment also contributed to a framework for continued coordination between the agencies as directed-energy systems are used in counter-drone operations.The Pentagon views the weapons as one component of a broader counter-drone network rather than a standalone solution. Directed-energy systems could complement other technologies by giving commanders additional options for responding to unmanned aircraft.The four systems selected in the current phase are not expected to be the only technologies considered. The Pentagon and JIATF-401 plan to continue evaluating other directed-energy systems for potential operational use.The task force is also preparing a directed-energy “shoot-off” at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah in December. Additional high-energy laser and high-powered microwave systems will be assessed during the event, with the results expected to help identify technologies that could be suitable for future deployment.The December evaluation will give the Defense Department another opportunity to compare systems under operationally relevant conditions as it expands its assessment of directed-energy weapons for counter-drone missions.

title: New US hypersonic cruise missile built to exceed Mach 5 enters tests
content: The U.S. Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) has started flight testing after the Royal Australian Air Force released a test unit over an Australian range. A report confirmed this on October 5, 2026, calling it a major milestone for a program that has faced several delays. The Air Force has not said when the release happened or if the missile flew on its own power afterwards.The development comes as the Air Force works toward a potential rapid acquisition decision in fiscal year 2027. It has also cut the rapid-prototyping campaign from seven flight tests to five.Australia hosts the testThe U.S. and Royal Australian Air Force are working together on HACM through the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment (SCIFiRE), a project built on more than 15 years of partnership.“The U.S. Air Force, in partnership with Australia, has conducted a flight test of the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) as part of our continuous work to advance long-range strike capabilities,” an Air Force spokesperson confirmed to The War Zone (TWZ). “This effort is part of the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment (SCIFiRE), a collaborative agreement built on more than 15 years of partnership between our two nations.”The Air Force has not shared the location or date of the test. It is also not clear which aircraft carried the HACM or if the missile’s scramjet engine worked after release. Earlier reports said the RAAF F/A-18F Super Hornet was expected to be used for testing.Inside the hypersonic designHACM is based on DARPA’s Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept (HAWC). In 2022, Raytheon, now called RTX, and Northrop Grumman were chosen to develop the missile.The weapon uses a rocket booster to reach the speed needed for its scramjet-powered cruiser to operate. The cruiser then separates from the booster and continues toward its target.“The missile consists of two stages, a rocket booster and a scramjet cruiser, which separates from the booster and eventually dives toward its target,” according to Government Accountability Office (GAO).HACM is designed for speeds above Mach 5, the standard threshold for hypersonic flight. Its maximum speed has not been disclosed.The flight schedule slippedHACM was originally expected to begin flight testing in 2024. The target moved to 2025 and then to fiscal year 2026. A July 2026 GAO report said the program was on track for its first flight test in the second quarter of fiscal year 2026, a period that ended on March 31, 2026.That planned window has therefore passed. The October announcement confirms that a flight-test release has occurred, but it does not state when the event happened.“The HACM program is on track to conduct its first flight test in the second quarter of fiscal year 2026, but officials said there is effectively zero margin left in the schedule for the rapid prototyping effort. The program has already descoped the rapid prototyping effort from seven to five planned flight tests,” GAO said in a July report.Five tests remainThe shortened campaign leaves little room for failure as the Air Force targets a fiscal 2027 procurement decision.“If a significant flight test failure occurs, it is likely that the program will not be able to complete all five tests within the 5-year rapid prototyping timeframe,” the report continued. “According to the program, completing at least the first three flight tests is critical for informing the Air Force’s decision to initiate a rapid fielding effort and procure HACM in fiscal year 2027.”The program has also taken risks to preserve its schedule. The confirmed Australian release now moves HACM into its long-awaited flight-test phase, while the Air Force faces the challenge of completing the remaining tests in time to support its 2027 acquisition plans.

title: NASA upgrades wind tunnel to study dangerous supercooled ice on jets
content: NASA’s Glenn Research Center is using its Icing Research Tunnel to study “supercooled large droplet icing.”In aviation, tiny things can trigger massive trouble. High above the clouds, ultra-chilled liquid water that refuses to freeze poses a hidden hazard to passing aircraft. Known as supercooled large droplet icing, this rare phenomenon happens when large drops remain liquid in sub-freezing temperatures. The moment these droplets slam into a plane’s wing, they flash-freeze.That’s why NASA researchers are upgrading their legendary Icing Research Tunnel to crack the physics behind these treacherous airborne traps. Mapping these droplets could help improve airplane design tools and protect pilots during dangerous weather conditions.Aviation hazardAircraft icing is one of the major severe cold-weather hazards. In some extreme situations, it can even rapidly escalate. Even with certified ice-protection systems engaged, ice can still accumulate on unprotected surfaces. This unexpected buildup can threaten lift and flight controllability before crews recognize and respond to the danger.Standard cloud droplets measure only 2 to 100 microns wide, allowing standard aircraft de-icing systems to manage them easily. Supercooled large droplets present a far greater threat because they can reach sizes up to 2,000 microns. Instead of simply freezing on contact, these oversized drops splash across the aircraft surface. That liquid splatter slides past protected wing edges and coats vulnerable, unprotected areas in ice.Existing engineering tools struggle to model this complex fluid behavior.To fix the blind spot, NASA engineers are testing advanced optical “probes” inside their specialized wind tunnel. These probes can capture drops larger than 45 microns and calculate their sizes instantly, replacing hours of grueling image processing. “NASA researchers have experimented with brand new probes that help calibrate the sizes of the drops in the clouds the tunnel produces. The probes can “see” drops larger than 45 microns and perform a real-time analysis of their sizes,” the space agency noted. Combining real-time readings with data from sensors that monitor smaller droplets lets scientists map the full spray spectrum in detail. Upgrading the Icing Research Tunnel lets engineers collect the vital ground-testing data needed to meet these stringent regulatory requirements without dangerous flight tests.The path to safer flights This research is crucial for NASA because it directly advances its core civil aviation mission to make air travel safer, smarter, and more efficient.Tragic incidents like the 1994 Roselawn crash prompted aviation authorities such as the FAA and EASA to establish strict certification standards. As a result, aircraft manufacturers must now prove their planes can safely navigate or quickly escape supercooled large droplet icing conditions. Designed to accommodate full-scale components and sub-scale models, the IRT’s precise controls simulate extreme environmental conditions with adjustable air velocities, sub-freezing temperatures, and standardized droplet distributions. Major aerospace defense entities and commercial manufacturers use this infrastructure to fulfill rigorous certification requirements without resorting to dangerous flight testing.In addition, avionics developers are creating real-time sensors, including optical, capacitive, and acoustic systems, to identify droplets splashing beyond protected leading edges. NASA’s cloud measurement data provides the calibration needed for these cockpit warning systems. Accurate calibration ensures these systems trigger immediate pilot alerts before ice accumulation compromises flight safety.

title: World’s largest fusion reactor gets final 485-ton vacuum vessel sector
content: ITER, the world’s largest nuclear fusion reactor, reached a major milestone in its decades-long journey after a European consortium delivered the final vacuum vessel sector on site. The vacuum vessel is also known as the plasma chamber and will be home to fusion reactions while also acting as the first containment barrier for the reactor. In our bid to move away from fossil fuels, scientists are working to replicate the reactions that occur in stars and release large amounts of carbon-free energy in the process. Called nuclear fusion, the process is considered advantageous over its fission counterpart, since it does not generate large amounts of radioactive waste. However, nuclear fusion research is still in its infancy, and scientists are working to create reactions that can be sustained for long durations. ITER is the world’s largest nuclear fusion experiment that is working to sustain nuclear fusion reactions inside a tokamak, or donut-shaped, reactor vessel. A collaborative effort between 35 nations, the facility is being built at Saint-Paul-lès-Durance in southern France and reached a major milestone with the delivery of the ninth and final sector of its vacuum vessel or plasma chamber. ITER’s Vacuum VesselThe vacuum vessel is a key component of a tokamak fusion reactor. Made of stainless steel, the vessel provides a clean environment for fusion reactions. It provides a scaffold for superconducting magnets to be placed and to control the plasma movements. ITER’s design of the vacuum vessel consists of nine sectors which, when joined together, will boast an internal volume of 49,440 cubic feet (1,400 cubic meters). Each of these sectors are about 46 feet (14 m) tall. Each sector weighs about 485 U.S. tons (440 tonnes) and is built in four segments, requiring over 5,250 feet (1,600 m) of welding assembly. When assembled, the vacuum vessel will have a diameter of 63 feet (19.4 m) and, along with other vessel components such as the blanket and the diverter, will weigh 9369 U.S. tons (8,500 tonnes). The manufacturing of sectors for the vacuum vessel was shared between Europe and South Korea, with the latter producing four of these sectors. A European consortium was tasked with manufacturing five of these sectors, the last of which was delivered last week. Who built ITER sectors in Europe?The sectors were built by the AMW consortium, which consists of Ansaldo Nucleare, Westinghouse Electric Company and Walter Tosto, alongside 15 other companies in the supply chain. Manufacturing the five sectors took more than two million hours of work and 466 miles (750 km) of welding beads. The production of the four segments of each sector was carried out at Westinghouse, Monfalcone, and in Walter Tosto, Chieti and then welded together. Once ready, the sector was shipped and then travelled by land before reaching ITER’s assembly site in southern France. “Vacuum vessel sector #2 represents the last of our core tokamak components—now all toroidal field coils, poloidal field coils, correction coils, central solenoid magnets, vacuum vessel sectors and thermal shield sets are on site,” said Pietro Barabaschi, ITER Director General, after receiving delivery of the final sector in a press release.
